pr_summary: Adds basic nonnegativity/cast lemmas for `ArchimedeanClass.mk`, explicit `FiniteElement.mk` simp lemmas, a rational-cast computation in the finite residue field, and several standard-part theorems including zero/nonzero criteria, monotonicity on finite elements, special add/sub formulas when one summand is infinitesimal, and a streamlined rational-cast formula.

declarations.name: ArchimedeanClass.mk_intCast_nonneg
declarations.nl_statement: For any integer `n`, the Archimedean class of `(n : S)` is nonnegative.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Split on `n = 0` or `n ≠ 0`. In the zero case, simplify. In the nonzero case, use the existing theorem `mk_intCast` saying the class is actually `0`, so nonnegativity is immediate.
declarations.divergence: Very direct case split matching the mathematical idea exactly.

declarations.name: ArchimedeanClass.mk_natCast_nonneg
declarations.nl_statement: For any natural number `n`, the Archimedean class of `(n : S)` is nonnegative.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Obtain the result by `mod_cast` from the integer version `mk_intCast_nonneg`. So the proof is entirely a coercion transfer.
declarations.divergence: Extremely short; the math is transparent if one is comfortable with `mod_cast`.

declarations.name: ArchimedeanClass.mk_ratCast_nonneg
declarations.nl_statement: For any rational `q`, the Archimedean class of `(q : R)` is nonnegative.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again split into `q = 0` and `q ≠ 0`. The zero case is by simplification; the nonzero case rewrites with `mk_ratCast`, which gives value `0`.
declarations.divergence: Same clean pattern as the integer lemma, with no Lean-specific detours besides the case split.

declarations.name: FiniteElement.mk_add
declarations.nl_statement: If `x` and `y` are finite elements (expressed by hypotheses `0 ≤ mk x` and `0 ≤ mk y`), then the sum of the corresponding `FiniteElement.mk`s is definitionally the finite element represented by `x + y`, with the standard proof that `x + y` is finite.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is `rfl`: the additive structure on `FiniteElement` was defined so that adding the subtype representatives produces exactly this term with the displayed proof of finiteness.
declarations.divergence: Completely direct once one knows the structure definitions, but it relies on definitional unfolding rather than an explanatory argument.

declarations.name: FiniteElement.mk_sub
declarations.nl_statement: Under the same finiteness hypotheses, subtraction of finite elements is represented by subtraction of the underlying field elements.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Also `rfl`: subtraction in `FiniteElement` is defined componentwise, and the finiteness proof is the standard bound coming from `min_le_mk_sub`.
declarations.divergence: Same as `mk_add`: transparent to a Lean reader who knows the definitions, but mostly definitional.

declarations.name: FiniteElement.mk_mul
declarations.nl_statement: If `x` and `y` are finite, then the product of the corresponding finite elements is represented by `x * y`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again `rfl`: multiplication on `FiniteElement` is defined on representatives, and the proof that the product is finite is exactly `add_nonneg hx hy`.
declarations.divergence: Pure definitional computation; quite readable.

declarations.name: FiniteElement.mk_le_mk_iff
declarations.nl_statement: For finite representatives `x` and `y`, ordering their `FiniteElement.mk`s is equivalent to ordering `x` and `y` in `K`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is definitionally true for the subtype order, so the proof is `.rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence; a literal restatement of the subtype order.

declarations.name: FiniteElement.mk_lt_mk_iff
declarations.nl_statement: For finite representatives `x` and `y`, strict inequality of their `FiniteElement.mk`s is equivalent to strict inequality of `x` and `y` in `K`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Also `.rfl`, since the strict order on the subtype is inherited directly from `K`.
declarations.divergence: Again purely definitional.

declarations.name: FiniteElement.instCoeRat
declarations.nl_statement: Defines the coercion from rationals into `FiniteElement K` by sending `q` to the finite element represented by `q`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The definition is just `q ↦ FiniteElement.mk q (mk_ratCast_nonneg q)`, using the new nonnegativity lemma to show rational numbers are finite.
declarations.divergence: A direct definition with no hidden maneuvering.

declarations.name: FiniteResidueField.mk_ratCast
declarations.nl_statement: The residue-field image of a rational number, viewed as a finite element, is exactly that rational number in `FiniteResidueField K`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Write the rational as `n / d` with `d ≠ 0`. Multiply both sides by `d` and use left-cancellation (`mul_left_inj'`) to reduce to proving equality after scaling. Rewrite the scaled left-hand side using ring-hom properties of `mk`, the explicit `FiniteElement.mk_natCast`, and `FiniteElement.mk_mul`; after these rewrites, `simp_all` reduces the statement to the obvious arithmetic identity.
declarations.divergence: Mathematically natural—clear denominator by multiplying by `d`—but the Lean proof is somewhat compressed and depends on several coercion and simp rewrites packed into one `rw`/`simp_all` block.

declarations.name: stdPart_eq_zero_iff
declarations.nl_statement: For any `x : K`, the standard part of `x` is zero iff `mk x ≠ 0`, i.e. iff `x` is not infinitesimally close to a nonzero finite residue class.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The backward direction is exactly the earlier theorem `stdPart_of_mk_ne_zero`. For the forward direction, prove the contrapositive: if `mk x = 0`, then `0 ≤ mk x`, so the standard-part definition uses the finite branch. Rewrite with `stdPart_of_mk_nonneg`, then use that the chosen embedding into `ℝ` preserves nonzeroness (`map_ne_zero`) together with `FiniteResidueField.mk_ne_zero` to conclude the standard part is nonzero.
declarations.divergence: Conceptually direct, but the `contrapose!` plus transport through the residue field and embedding adds some Lean-specific infrastructure.

declarations.name: stdPart_ne_zero_iff
declarations.nl_statement: For any `x : K`, the standard part is nonzero iff `mk x = 0`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is obtained immediately from `stdPart_eq_zero_iff` by negating both sides (`ne_left`).
declarations.divergence: A clean logical reformulation with no extra proof content.

declarations.name: stdPart_monotoneOn
declarations.nl_statement: `stdPart` is monotone on the set of elements `x` with `0 ≤ mk x`, i.e. on finite elements.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Take `x ≤ y` with both finiteness hypotheses. Unfold `stdPart`, so both sides reduce to the finite branch. Then apply monotonicity of the order ring homomorphism from `FiniteElement K` to `ℝ`; the needed inequality between finite elements is exactly the original `x ≤ y`, rewritten via `FiniteElement.mk_le_mk_iff`.
declarations.divergence: This closely follows the mathematical map-is-monotone argument; only the final rewrite through the subtype lemma is Lean-specific.

declarations.name: stdPart_add
declarations.nl_statement: If `x` and `y` are finite (`0 ≤ mk x`, `0 ≤ mk y`), then `stdPart (x + y) = stdPart x + stdPart y`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unfold `stdPart`; all three occurrences are in the finite branch by the hypotheses and the finiteness of `x+y`. Then the claim is exactly preservation of addition by the composite order ring homomorphism, applied to the finite representatives.
declarations.divergence: A textbook homomorphism argument rendered directly in Lean.

declarations.name: stdPart_add_of_mk_neg_left
declarations.nl_statement: If `0 < mk x` (so `x` is infinitesimal in the sense that its standard part vanishes), then `stdPart (x + y) = stdPart y`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Split on whether `y` is finite (`0 ≤ mk y`) or infinitesimal-negative (`0 < mk y` under the order trichotomy used here). If `y` is finite, use `stdPart_add hx.le hy` and then `stdPart_of_mk_ne_zero hx.ne'` to replace `stdPart x` by `0`. If `y` is not finite, then both `stdPart y` and `stdPart (x+y)` are zero by `stdPart_of_mk_ne_zero`; for the latter, show `mk (x+y) ≠ 0` by rewriting with `mk_add_eq_mk_right (hy.trans hx)` and using `hy.ne`.
declarations.divergence: The mathematical idea is simple—an infinitesimal summand does not change standard part—but the proof’s split into two valuation-sign cases and the use of `mk_add_eq_mk_right` make the Lean script noticeably more specialized.

declarations.name: stdPart_add_of_mk_neg_right
declarations.nl_statement: If `0 < mk y`, then `stdPart (x + y) = stdPart x`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Commute the sum and apply the previous left-sided theorem.
declarations.divergence: Completely direct symmetry argument.

declarations.name: stdPart_sub
declarations.nl_statement: If `x` and `y` are finite, then `stdPart (x - y) = stdPart x - stdPart y`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite subtraction as addition of the negation on both sides, apply `stdPart_add`, and then use `stdPart_neg`; the finiteness hypothesis for `-y` comes from rewriting via `mk_neg`.
declarations.divergence: Very close to the standard mathematical reduction `x-y = x+(-y)`.

declarations.name: stdPart_sub_of_mk_neg_left
declarations.nl_statement: If `0 < mk x`, then `stdPart (x - y) = - stdPart y`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite `x - y` as `x + (-y)`, apply `stdPart_add_of_mk_neg_left` to kill the `x` term, and then simplify with `stdPart_neg`.
declarations.divergence: A short and faithful reduction to the previous addition theorem.

declarations.name: stdPart_sub_of_mk_neg_right
declarations.nl_statement: If `0 < mk y`, then `stdPart (x - y) = stdPart x`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again rewrite `x - y` as `x + (-y)` and apply the right-sided addition theorem to `-y`; the required positivity hypothesis is discharged by `simpa`.
declarations.divergence: Direct, with only a tiny coercion/sign simplification.

declarations.name: stdPart_ratCast
declarations.nl_statement: The standard part of a rational number in `K` is the same rational number.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Since rationals are finite, apply `stdPart_of_mk_nonneg` to move into the finite branch. Then compute the residue-field class of the rational using `FiniteResidueField.mk_ratCast`, and finally use that the chosen embedding from the residue field to `ℝ` preserves rational casts (`map_ratCast`).
declarations.divergence: Cleaner than the old denominator-based proof; it follows the conceptual factorization through the finite residue field very directly.

declarations.name: stdPart_intCast
declarations.nl_statement: The standard part of an integer is that integer.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Transfer the rational-cast theorem to integers via `mod_cast`.
declarations.divergence: A concise coercion-based corollary.

declarations.name: stdPart_natCast
declarations.nl_statement: The standard part of a natural number is that natural number.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Likewise obtained from the integer version by `mod_cast`.
declarations.divergence: Same direct coercion argument as above.

pr_summary: This PR adds two lemmas showing that continuity within a set, and hence ordinary continuity, is automatic at points that are not accumulation points of the relevant set/filter of points.

declarations.name: ContinuousWithinAt.of_not_accPt
declarations.nl_statement: If `x` is not an accumulation point of the set `s`, then any function `f` is continuous at `x` when restricted to `s`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof first rewrites continuity within `s` as continuity within `s \ {x}` using the existing equivalence `continuousWithinAt_diff_self`. So it is enough to show continuity on the punctured set. After unfolding `ContinuousWithinAt` and `AccPt`, and rewriting neighborhoods within intersections via `nhdsWithin_inter'`, the goal becomes a filter statement that follows directly from the assumption that `x` is not an accumulation point of `s`: on `s \ {x}` there are no points of `s` approaching `x`, so the source filter is trivial and any map tends to any target filter. The closing `simp_all` performs exactly these definitional reductions and filter simplifications.
declarations.divergence: Moderate-low. The mathematical idea is very direct—remove the point itself, then use that the punctured neighborhood filter is trivial when `x` is not an accumulation point—but the Lean proof compresses all substantive work into a single `simp_all` after several non-obvious rewrites and unfolds. So it follows the intended argument closely, but somewhat opaquely.

declarations.name: ContinuousAt.of_not_accPt
declarations.nl_statement: If `x` is isolated, i.e. `x` is not an accumulation point of `{x}ᶜ`, then any function `f` is continuous at `x`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite ordinary continuity `ContinuousAt f x` as continuity within the complement `{x}ᶜ` using `continuousWithinAt_compl_self`. Then apply the previous lemma `ContinuousWithinAt.of_not_accPt` with `s = {x}ᶜ`.
declarations.divergence: Very low. The Lean proof is exactly the two-step mathematical argument: convert `ContinuousAt` to `ContinuousWithinAt` on the punctured neighborhood and invoke the previous lemma.

pr_summary: Adds the star-algebra analogue of the continuous/endomorphism innerness theorem: every continuous ⋆-algebra equivalence between algebras of continuous endomorphisms of Hilbert spaces is conjugation by a linear isometry, together with the induced conjugation equivalence and a bridge turning continuous algebra equivalences from continuous algebra equivalences when continuity is supplied.

declarations.name: ContinuousLinearMap.LinearIsometryEquiv.conjStarAlgEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: A linear isometric equivalence between Hilbert spaces induces a ⋆-algebra equivalence between their algebras of continuous endomorphisms, given by conjugation.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The definition reuses the existing continuous-algebra conjugation equivalence attached to the underlying continuous linear equivalence, then proves the extra star-compatibility condition. That verification is a one-line `simp`: `star` on endomorphisms is adjoint, adjoint reverses composition, and for a linear isometry equivalence the inverse is the adjoint, so conjugation commutes with `star`.
declarations.divergence: Very direct: the Lean code is essentially the mathematical construction plus a single simplification proving preservation of adjoints.

declarations.name: ContinuousLinearMap.LinearIsometryEquiv.conjStarAlgEquiv_apply_apply
declarations.nl_statement: Evaluating the conjugation ⋆-algebra equivalence induced by an isometry `e` on an endomorphism `x` and a vector `y` gives `e (x (e.symm y))`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is just definitional unfolding of conjugation by `e`, so the proof is `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence; it is literally the defining formula.

declarations.name: ContinuousLinearMap.LinearIsometryEquiv.symm_conjStarAlgEquiv_apply_apply
declarations.nl_statement: The inverse conjugation equivalence acts by `e.symm (f (e x))`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again this is simply the definition of the inverse conjugation map, so the proof is `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence.

declarations.name: ContinuousLinearMap.LinearIsometryEquiv.conjStarAlgEquiv_apply
declarations.nl_statement: As an endomorphism-valued identity, `e.conjStarAlgEquiv x = e ∘L x ∘L e.symm`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is another definitional expansion of the conjugation construction, proved by `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence.

declarations.name: ContinuousLinearMap.LinearIsometryEquiv.symm_conjStarAlgEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: The inverse of the conjugation ⋆-algebra equivalence induced by `e` is the conjugation ⋆-algebra equivalence induced by `e.symm`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The statement follows directly from how the conjugation equivalence was defined, so the proof is `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence.

declarations.name: ContinuousLinearMap.LinearIsometryEquiv.conjStarAlgEquiv_refl
declarations.nl_statement: Conjugation by the identity isometry is the identity ⋆-algebra equivalence.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is immediate from the definition, hence `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence.

declarations.name: ContinuousLinearMap.LinearIsometryEquiv.conjStarAlgEquiv_trans
declarations.nl_statement: Conjugation by a composite isometry equals the composite of the corresponding conjugation ⋆-algebra equivalences.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Both sides reduce definitionally to the same conjugation formula, so the proof is `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence.

declarations.name: ContinuousAlgEquiv.ofAlgEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: An algebra equivalence can be regarded as a continuous algebra equivalence once continuity of it and its inverse are supplied.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The definition simply extends the given `AlgEquiv` structure with the two continuity fields.
declarations.divergence: Essentially none; it is a structure literal mirroring the statement.

declarations.name: ContinuousAlgEquiv.coe_ofAlgEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: The underlying function of `ofAlgEquiv e he he'` is just `e`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Since `ofAlgEquiv` only adds continuity fields, coercion to function is definitionally unchanged; proof is `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence.

declarations.name: ContinuousAlgEquiv.toAlgEquiv_ofAlgEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: For `ofAlgEquiv`, forgetting back to an algebra equivalence recovers the original `AlgEquiv`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again definitional: the new object was built from `e` by only adding continuity data, so the proof is `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence.

declarations.name: ContinuousAlgEquiv.ofAlgEquiv_toAlgEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: Starting from a continuous algebra equivalence, forgetting to an algebra equivalence and rebuilding with its continuity data gives back the original object.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is a definitional η-law for the structure, proved by `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence.

declarations.name: ContinuousAlgEquiv.symm_ofAlgEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: The inverse of `ofAlgEquiv e he he'` is `ofAlgEquiv e.symm he' he`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Both sides are the same structure after unfolding definitions, so the proof is `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence.

declarations.name: ContinuousAlgEquiv.ofAlgEquiv_trans_ofAlgEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: Composing two `ofAlgEquiv` constructions is the same as applying `ofAlgEquiv` to the composite, with the obvious composed continuity proofs.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The composition law is definitional for the structures involved, so the proof is `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence beyond bookkeeping the continuity arguments.

declarations.name: ContinuousAlgEquiv.auxContinuousLinearEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: Given a continuous linear equivalence `e` and scalars `α, α'` with `α'² = α⁻¹`, together with identities `e† e = α·id` and `e e† = α·id`, construct a rescaled continuous linear equivalence with forward map `α' • e` and inverse `α' • e†`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The definition specifies the forward and inverse linear maps as the scalar rescalings. To prove they are inverses, it evaluates the assumed operator identities pointwise, rewrites scalar multiplications, and uses `α' * α' = α⁻¹` and `α ≠ 0` to collapse the scalar factor to `1`. Continuity is inherited from continuity of scalar multiples of continuous linear maps.
declarations.divergence: Still close to the mathematics, but Lean has to shuttle between operator equalities and pointwise equalities via `congr`, and the scalar normalization is hidden inside `simp`.

declarations.name: ContinuousAlgEquiv.coe_auxContinuousLinearEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: The continuous linear map underlying `auxContinuousLinearEquiv` is exactly `α' • e`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is by definition of the structure, so `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence.

declarations.name: ContinuousAlgEquiv.auxIsometry
declarations.nl_statement: Under the same hypotheses, plus the fact that `α'` is self-conjugate, the rescaled continuous linear equivalence is actually a linear isometry equivalence.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof takes the linear equivalence part from `auxContinuousLinearEquiv`. For norm preservation it invokes the characterization `norm_map_iff_adjoint_comp_self`. The adjoint of `α' • e` is rewritten as `star α' • e†`; since `α'` is fixed by conjugation, the composite becomes `(α' * α') • (e† ∘ e)`. Using the assumed identity `e† ∘ e = α • id` and the relation `α'² = α⁻¹`, this simplifies to `1`, which is exactly the isometry criterion.
declarations.divergence: Mathematically faithful, but the Lean proof is compressed into a sequence of rewrites through coercions between continuous linear equivalences, linear equivalences, and semilinear scalar-action lemmas, so it reads less transparently than the argument.

declarations.name: ContinuousAlgEquiv.coe_auxIsometry
declarations.nl_statement: The continuous linear map underlying `auxIsometry` is `α' • e`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is definitional after unpacking `auxIsometry`, so `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence.

declarations.name: ContinuousAlgEquiv.coe_symm_auxIsometry
declarations.nl_statement: The continuous linear map underlying the inverse of `auxIsometry` is `α'⁻¹ • e.symm`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof extensionality-reduces to showing the two candidate inverses agree after composing with the forward map of the isometry, then uses injectivity of the constructed equivalence. A final simplification turns the scalar factors into `1` using invertibility of `α'`.
declarations.divergence: The mathematics is simple—rescaling the inverse by the reciprocal scalar—but Lean proves it indirectly via injectivity and simplification, which obscures the conceptual reason a bit.

declarations.name: StarAlgEquiv.eq_linearIsometryEquivConjStarAlgEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: A continuous ⋆-algebra equivalence between algebras of continuous endomorphisms of Hilbert spaces is conjugation by some linear isometry equivalence.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: First handle the subsingleton edge cases separately. Otherwise, use the previously proved continuous-algebra theorem to obtain a continuous linear equivalence `y` such that `f` is conjugation by `y`. Since `f` preserves adjoints, comparing `adjoint (f x)` with `f (adjoint x)` and expanding the conjugation formula shows that `y† y` commutes with every endomorphism. By centrality of the endomorphism algebra, `y† y = α · id` for some scalar `α`. The proof then shows: (1) `α` is real, because `y† y` is self-adjoint; (2) `α ≠ 0`, because `y† y` is invertible; (3) `α > 0`, because `y† y` is positive. A short calculation gives also `y y† = α · id`. Set `αa = (re α)^(-1/2)`, so `αa^2 = α⁻¹`. The auxiliary construction then turns `αa • y` into a linear isometry `U`. Finally, expanding `U.conjStarAlgEquiv` and cancelling the scalar factors shows that conjugation by `U` equals the original `f`.
declarations.divergence: The underlying strategy is clearly explained in the proof comment and does match the mathematics, but the formal proof is considerably longer and more indirect: it threads through `ContinuousAlgEquiv.ofAlgEquiv`, rewrites star-preservation into a commuting statement, uses center machinery to extract the scalar, proves reality/positivity through `IsSelfAdjoint` and `isPositive` lemmas, and handles the scalar normalization with `Real.rpow`/`norm_num`. The argument is faithful but not especially transparent line-by-line.

declarations.name: instOrderIsoClass
declarations.nl_statement: Any class of continuous star-preserving algebra equivalences between endomorphism algebras is automatically an `OrderIsoClass`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Given such an equivalence `f`, the previous theorem expresses it as conjugation by a linear isometry `U`. Order on these operator algebras is defined via positivity of differences, so the proof rewrites `f a` as `U`-conjugation, transports `x ≤ y` to positivity of `y - x`, and then uses the existing theorem that positivity is preserved and reflected under conjugation by a linear isometry. This yields `f x ≤ f y ↔ x ≤ y`.
declarations.divergence: Conceptually direct, but Lean first coerces the equivalence-class element to an actual `StarAlgEquiv`, invokes continuity via a typeclass, and then rewrites order through `le_def` and positivity lemmas; so the proof is concise but somewhat infrastructure-heavy.

pr_summary: This PR replaces `addConstInfo` with `addTermInfo'` at several points where commands or attributes create or refer to declarations from defining syntax, so editor hover/go-to information is attached as binder/definition-site info and shows up correctly in VSCode.

declarations.name: higherOrderGetParam
declarations.nl_statement: Given a theorem tagged with the `higher_order` attribute, parse the optional generated name, build the corresponding higher-order version of the theorem, add it to the environment, and register editor/simp metadata for the new declaration.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: After choosing the output name, the code enters `MetaM`/`TermElabM`, reads the original theorem’s universe parameters and type, and computes the desired higher-order target type. It then constructs a proof term by creating a metavariable for that target, introducing the outer binders, applying `funext` to reduce function equality to pointwise equality, introducing the resulting point, and applying the original theorem; all remaining goals are discharged by assumptions. The finished metavariable is instantiated and packaged as a theorem declaration. The rest of the function only records source ranges, term info, and simp/functor-norm registrations.
declarations.divergence: The proof construction closely matches the mathematical idea “prove extensional equality by `funext`, then apply the original pointwise theorem”, though it is expressed through metavariable operations rather than a direct term.

declarations.name: mkIffOfInductivePropImpl
declarations.nl_statement: For an inductively defined proposition `ind`, construct and add a theorem `rel` expressing `ind ... ↔` a disjunction over its constructors, with existential/equality conditions encoding each constructor’s arguments and indices.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The function first checks that the input is an inductive proposition, extracts its constructors and parameters, and constructs the theorem statement by opening the inductive type telescope and, for each constructor, translating that constructor into one disjunct via `constrToProp`; the right-hand side is the disjunction of these constructor descriptions. To prove the theorem, it creates a goal for the full `iff`, introduces all variables, and applies `Iff.intro`, producing the two directions. The forward direction is solved by `toCases`, which performs case analysis on a proof of the inductive proposition and places the result into the appropriate disjunct. For the reverse direction, it introduces a proof of the disjunction and calls `toInductive`, which reconstructs a proof of the inductive proposition from the chosen constructor data. Finally it adds the theorem and records syntax metadata.
declarations.divergence: The high-level argument is standard and fairly direct, but substantial work is delegated to helper procedures (`constrToProp`, `toCases`, `toInductive`), so the proof script is more of a compact orchestration than a transparent step-by-step derivation.

declarations.name: addProjection
declarations.nl_statement: Given expressions `lhs` and `rhs` of the same type together with their local parameters, create and register a theorem named `declName` asserting `lhs = rhs`, optionally simplifying the right-hand side first and attaching the configured attributes.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The function begins with the reflexivity proof of `lhs = lhs`. If the configuration requests simplification of the right-hand side, it runs `dsimp` and then `simp` on `rhs`, updating both the rewritten expression and the accompanying proof. It then forms the universally quantified equality theorem over the supplied arguments, checks the environment to ensure the name is fresh, and adds the theorem declaration using the proof term accumulated above. Afterward it infers definitional-equality attributes, attaches source/term info, optionally adds the theorem to the simp extension, and applies any extra user-specified attributes.
declarations.divergence: This mirrors the intended construction very closely: simplify `rhs`, keep the proof certificate produced by simplification, then abstract over the arguments and register the resulting equality theorem.

declarations.name: addTranslationAttr
declarations.nl_statement: Implement the translation attribute (such as `to_additive`-style infrastructure) by determining the target name for a source declaration, checking whether the target already exists, creating or updating the translation and metadata, and finally attaching editor information for the translated declaration.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The function first rejects non-global uses, then checks whether the source has already been translated. If so, it either updates reorder/relevant-argument metadata after validating compatibility, or errors out. Otherwise it computes the target name, checks whether it already exists, validates the `existing` option, computes argument-reordering information, and inserts the translation entry. pr_summary: This PR adds the theorem that the Mahler measure of any cyclotomic polynomial, after mapping coefficients into ℂ, is equal to 1.

declarations.name: Polynomial.cyclotomic_mahlerMeasure_eq_one
declarations.nl_statement: For any commutative ring `R` equipped with an `R`-algebra structure on `ℂ`, and any natural number `n`, the polynomial obtained by mapping the `n`th cyclotomic polynomial from `R[X]` to `ℂ[X]` has Mahler measure equal to `1`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof splits into the special case `n = 0` and the main case `n ≠ 0`. When `n = 0`, the result is discharged by simplification. For `n ≠ 0`, it rewrites the Mahler measure using the standard formula `‖leadingCoeff‖ * ∏ max 1 ‖root‖`. It also rewrites the mapped cyclotomic polynomial as the complex cyclotomic polynomial, uses that cyclotomic polynomials are monic so the leading-coefficient factor is `1`, and simplifies `max 1 ‖ζ‖` to `1` whenever `ζ` is unitary. Thus it remains to show that every root contributes the factor `1`. The roots of `cyclotomic n ℂ` are rewritten as the multiset of primitive `n`th roots of unity; for each such root, `isPrimitiveRoot_of_mem_primitiveRoots` shows it is primitive, and `IsPrimitiveRoot.norm'_eq_one` gives `‖ζ‖ = 1` (using `n ≠ 0` to obtain `NeZero (n : ℂ)`). Hence every term in the product is `1`, so the whole product is `1`.
declarations.divergence: The Lean proof follows the textbook argument very closely: reduce to the product-over-roots formula, identify cyclotomic roots as primitive roots of unity, and use that primitive roots of unity lie on the unit circle. The only noticeable proof-engineering overhead is the explicit `n = 0` case split and the construction of `NeZero (n : ℂ)` from `n ≠ 0`, plus some simplification lemmas (`map_cyclotomic`, `norm_of_mem_unitary`, `Multiset.prod_eq_one`).

pr_summary: This PR removes explicit `[NeZero n]` assumptions from several `Fin` lemmas whose hypotheses already contain an element of `Fin n`, deriving nonzeroness internally from that element.

declarations.name: neZero_of_exists
declarations.nl_statement: For any `i : Fin n`, the natural number `n` is nonzero.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unfold `NeZero n` as `n ≠ 0`. Assume `n = 0`; rewriting that equality in the hypothesis turns `i` into an element of `Fin 0`, which is impossible, so `i.elim0` closes the contradiction.
declarations.divergence: Very direct: it is exactly the mathematical argument that existence of an element of `Fin n` forces `n ≠ 0`.

declarations.name: castLT_sub_nezero
declarations.nl_statement: If `i < j` in `Fin n`, then after viewing `j - i` as an element of `Fin (n - i.val)` via the obvious upper-bound proof, that element is not `0`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: First install the needed instance `NeZero (n - i.val)` from the strict inequality `i < j`, since `j < n` implies `i.val < n`. To prove the casted difference is nonzero, it is enough to show its natural-number value is nonzero (`ne_of_val_ne`). The value computes to `j.val - i.val` because `i ≤ j`; arithmetic (`lia`) shows this is positive when `i < j`, and hence not zero.
declarations.divergence: Mostly direct, but slightly compressed: the proof routes through `ne_of_val_ne`, a simp normalization of subtraction, and `lia` rather than explicitly stating positivity of `j.val - i.val`.

declarations.name: one_le_of_ne_zero
declarations.nl_statement: Given `k : Fin n`, once one derives `NeZero n` from the existence of `k`, any hypothesis `k ≠ 0` implies `1 ≤ k`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Derive `NeZero n` from `k`. Rewrite `n` as a successor using `Nat.exists_eq_succ_of_ne_zero`. Then split on whether that predecessor is `0` or `succ _`. In the one-element case `Fin 1`, every element is `0`, so the implication is vacuous and simplifies to `0 ≤ 0`. In the larger case, reduce the inequality `1 ≤ k` to the statement that `k.val ≠ 0`, which is exactly the hypothesis `k ≠ 0` via `val_ne_zero_iff`.
declarations.divergence: The core idea is clear, but the proof is more case-splitting and representation-driven than the informal math; the `Fin 1` branch is discharged by simplification rather than being explained conceptually.

declarations.name: val_sub_one_of_ne_zero
declarations.nl_statement: Given `i : Fin n`, after deriving `NeZero n` from `i`, any hypothesis `i ≠ 0` implies that the value of `i - 1` is the ordinary natural subtraction `i.val - 1`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Derive `NeZero n` from `i` and rewrite `n` as a successor. Then use the standard formula for `Fin` subtraction under a proof `1 ≤ i`, obtaining `(i - 1).val = (i.val - 1) % n`. The needed lower bound `1 ≤ i` comes from the previous lemma `one_le_of_ne_zero`. Finally, show `i.val - 1 < n`, so the modulus disappears by `Nat.mod_eq_of_lt`; this bound is obtained from the fact that `i ≠ 0` makes `Fin n` nontrivial, hence `2 ≤ n`.
declarations.divergence: Reasonably faithful, but somewhat indirect: it depends on rewriting `n` as a successor, invoking the previous lemma for `1 ≤ i`, and using nontriviality-to-`2 ≤ n` machinery to justify dropping the modulus.

declarations.name: cast_val_eq_self
declarations.nl_statement: For any `a : Fin n`, after deriving `NeZero n` from `a`, coercing `a.val` back to `Fin n` gives back `a`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Derive `NeZero n` from `a`. Then extensionality reduces equality in `Fin n` to equality of underlying values. The value of `(a.val : Fin n)` is `a.val` by the earlier lemma `val_cast_of_lt`, using the bound `a.isLt`.

declarations.name: val_add_one_of_lt'
declarations.nl_statement: Given `i : Fin n`, after deriving `NeZero n` from `i`, if `i.val + 1 < n` then `(i + 1).val = i.val + 1`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Derive `NeZero n` from `i`. Expand `Fin` addition (`add_def`), so `(i + 1).val` is `(i.val + 1) % n`. The hypothesis says this sum is already below `n`, so `Nat.mod_eq_of_lt` removes the modulus. The side arithmetic is handled by `lia`.
declarations.divergence: Direct and transparent; the only compression is that `lia` packages the routine arithmetic needed to match the hypothesis to the mod-elimination lemma.

declarations.name: Measure.exists_innerRegular_eq_of_isCompact

pr_summary: This PR adds basic API lemmas computing covering and packing numbers for the empty set, singletons, and radius zero, plus simple comparison lemmas with `encard` and a simp lemma that every set is `0`-separated.

declarations.name: packingNumber_empty
declarations.nl_statement: The packing number of the empty set is `0` for every radius.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof is just `simp [packingNumber]`: after unfolding the definition, the relevant supremum over subsets of `∅` collapses to `0`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence; the Lean proof is exactly the one-line mathematical simplification.

declarations.name: packingNumber_eq_zero
declarations.nl_statement: A set has packing number `0` iff the set is empty.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unfold `packingNumber`, `ENat.iSup_eq_zero`, and `encard_eq_zero`. The reverse implication is immediate by simp. For the forward implication, argue by contradiction: if `A` is nonempty, choose `x ∈ A`; then the singleton `{x}` is a subset of `A`, is `ε`-separated, and has nonzero `encard`, contradicting that every term in the supremum is `0`.
declarations.divergence: Very close to the textbook argument; the only Lean-specific wrinkle is expressing 'supremum is zero' via `ENat.iSup_eq_zero` and feeding the singleton into the hypothesis.

declarations.name: packingNumber_pos
declarations.nl_statement: If `A` is nonempty, then its packing number is positive.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite positivity as being nonzero in `ENat`, then use `packingNumber_eq_zero`: a nonempty set is not empty, so its packing number cannot be `0`.
declarations.divergence: A concise corollary of the previous iff; slightly Lean-flavored because positivity is proved via `Ne.bot_lt`.

declarations.name: IsSeparated.encard_le_packingNumber
declarations.nl_statement: If `C ⊆ A` and `C` is `ε`-separated, then `C.encard ≤ packingNumber ε A`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unfold the definition of packing number as a supremum over subsets and separatedness proofs. Then apply the standard `iSup` lower-bound lemmas to the particular witness `C` together with the hypotheses `C ⊆ A` and `IsSeparated ε C`.
declarations.divergence: Essentially no divergence: this is the direct order-theoretic introduction rule for a supremum.

declarations.name: externalCoveringNumber_le_encard_self
declarations.nl_statement: The external covering number of `A` is at most `A.encard`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use the general lemma saying any cover gives an upper bound on the external covering number, and instantiate it with the trivial fact that `A` covers itself.
declarations.divergence: Direct reuse of a previously proved lemma; mirrors the mathematical proof exactly.

declarations.name: coveringNumber_le_encard_self
declarations.nl_statement: The covering number of `A` is at most `A.encard`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Apply the analogous lemma for covering numbers using the obvious inclusion `A ⊆ A` and the trivial self-cover of `A`.
declarations.divergence: Again completely direct: the proof is just the expected instantiation of the general bound.

declarations.name: packingNumber_le_encard_self
declarations.nl_statement: The packing number of `A` is at most `A.encard`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unfold `packingNumber` and prove every term in the supremum is at most `A.encard`. For any separated subset `C ⊆ A`, monotonicity of `encard` under inclusion gives `C.encard ≤ A.encard`; then conclude with `iSup_le_iff`.
declarations.divergence: Very close to the obvious argument; the only Lean-specific feature is the explicit `iSup_le_iff` reduction.

declarations.name: externalCoveringNumber_zero
declarations.nl_statement: In an extended metric space, the external covering number of radius `0` equals the cardinality `A.encard`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: For the upper bound, use `externalCoveringNumber_le_encard_self`. For the lower bound, show any `0`-covering set `C` must contain `A`: after rewriting the cover condition with `isCover_zero`, it becomes exactly an inclusion, so `A.encard ≤ C.encard` by monotonicity. Since the external covering number is the infimum of such `C.encard`, this gives the reverse inequality.
declarations.divergence: The mathematics is direct; the Lean proof is slightly more order-theoretic because it builds the lower bound by `le_iInf` over all covering sets and rewrites with `isCover_zero`.

declarations.name: coveringNumber_zero
declarations.nl_statement: In an extended metric space, the covering number of radius `0` equals `A.encard`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Upper bound: use `coveringNumber_le_encard_self`. Lower bound: identify `externalCoveringNumber 0 A` with `A.encard` via the previous lemma, then use the general inequality `externalCoveringNumber ≤ coveringNumber`.
declarations.divergence: A clean two-step reduction to previous lemmas; the only minor indirection is routing through external covering numbers.

declarations.name: packingNumber_zero
declarations.nl_statement: In an extended metric space, the packing number of radius `0` equals `A.encard`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Upper bound: use `packingNumber_le_encard_self`. Lower bound: observe that the whole set `A` itself is an admissible `0`-separated subset, because every set is `0`-separated; then the supremum defining `packingNumber 0 A` is at least `A.encard`.
declarations.divergence: Almost perfectly transparent. The Lean code compresses the lower bound into a single `le_iSup_of_le A (by simp)` using the new `isSeparated_zero` simp lemma.

declarations.name: coveringNumber_singleton
declarations.nl_statement: The covering number of a singleton is `1` for every radius.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Apply the existing lemma that any nonempty set of diameter at most `ε` has covering number `1`; a singleton is nonempty and has diameter `0`, hence diameter at most `ε`.
declarations.divergence: No real divergence; this is exactly the intended one-line specialization.

declarations.name: externalCoveringNumber_singleton
declarations.nl_statement: The external covering number of a singleton is `1` for every radius.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Specialize the corresponding 'diameter at most `ε` implies value `1`' lemma to the singleton, using its obvious nonemptiness and zero diameter.
declarations.divergence: Again a direct one-line specialization with no hidden complexity.

declarations.name: packingNumber_singleton
declarations.nl_statement: The packing number of a singleton is `1` for every radius.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: For the upper bound, combine `packingNumber_le_encard_self {x}` with `encard {x} = 1`. For the lower bound, exhibit `{x}` itself in the supremum defining the packing number: it is a subset of itself, it is `ε`-separated because pairwise conditions on a singleton are vacuous, and its cardinality is `1`.
declarations.divergence: Mathematically straightforward, but the Lean proof is somewhat terse and encoded as a chain of nested `le_iSup_of_le` calls with several `by simp` witnesses, so the structure is less immediately readable than the companion singleton lemmas.

declarations.name: isSeparated_zero
declarations.nl_statement: Every set in an extended metric space is `0`-separated.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unfold `IsSeparated` and `Set.Pairwise`; the condition becomes that for distinct points `x ≠ y`, one has `0 < edist x y`, which is exactly the standard simplification handled by `simp`.
declarations.divergence: Very direct; the proof is just definitional unfolding plus simplification.

pr_summary: This PR removes obsolete `backward.privateInPublic` settings and expired deprecated aliases, and makes a helper for connected components explicitly private without changing the substantive proofs.

declarations.name: ShortComplex.mapToComposableArrows_id
declarations.nl_statement: For a short complex `S₁`, sending the identity morphism of `S₁` to a morphism of composable arrows gives the identity morphism on `S₁.toComposableArrows`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof is just `cat_disch`, which discharges the categorical identity goal by unfolding the relevant categorical structure and reducing it to definitional equalities of the components. There is no real argument beyond functoriality-by-definition.
declarations.divergence: Virtually none: the Lean proof is the expected one-line categorical simplification.

declarations.name: ConnectedComponent.walk_toSimpleGraph'
declarations.nl_statement: Given a connected component `C` of a graph `G`, vertices `u,v ∈ C`, and a walk `p : G.Walk u v` in the original graph, one obtains a walk in the induced simple graph `C.toSimpleGraph` from `⟨u,hu⟩` to `⟨v,hv⟩`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof is by recursion on the walk `p`. If `p` is empty, return the empty walk. If `p` is a cons step `u -- w` followed by a walk from `w` to `v`, first show `w ∈ C` using closure of the support under adjacency, then reinterpret the original adjacency as an adjacency in `C.toSimpleGraph`, and finally prepend that edge to the recursively converted tail walk.
declarations.divergence: Very direct structural recursion on walks; the only Lean-specific overhead is packaging membership proofs for the subtype vertices.

declarations.name: ConnectedComponent.walk_toSimpleGraph
declarations.nl_statement: For any two vertices `u,v` in a connected component `C`, there is a walk between the corresponding vertices of `C.toSimpleGraph`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use the fact that any two vertices in the same connected component are reachable in the original graph. Choose a witness walk from that reachability statement using `.some`, then feed it into `walk_toSimpleGraph'` to transfer it to the induced graph on the component.
declarations.divergence: Completely standard mathematically; the only non-mathematical aspect is the noncomputable choice of a witness walk from an existential.

declarations.name: isBridge_iff_mem_and_forall_cycle_notMem
declarations.nl_statement: An edge `e` is a bridge iff it belongs to the graph’s edge set and is contained in no cycle of the graph.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The edge `e : Sym2 V` is reduced to an unordered pair of endpoints by `Sym2.ind`. After that reduction, the result is exactly the previously established theorem `isBridge_iff_adj_and_forall_cycle_notMem` for edges written as `s(v,w)`. So the proof is just induction on the quotient representation of `e` and reuse of the endpoint-based characterization.
declarations.divergence: Quite direct, but it depends on the Lean-specific quotient eliminator `Sym2.ind` to move from a general edge to a pair of vertices.

declarations.name: nil_notMem_splitByLoop
declarations.nl_statement: The auxiliary list-producing function `splitBy.loop` never outputs the empty list as one of its pieces when started with a current element `a` and accumulator `g`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Proceed by induction on the remaining input list `l`, generalizing over `a` and `g`. In the base case, simplification of `splitBy.loop` shows the result immediately. In the inductive step, unfold `splitBy.loop` and split on the Boolean branch deciding whether to extend the current chunk or break it. In the extending branch, apply the induction hypothesis directly. In the breaking branch, rewrite the result as an append and use membership in an append to reduce again to the induction hypothesis; simplification finishes.
declarations.divergence: The proof mirrors the recursive definition closely; the only extra Lean work is explicit rewriting with the append form and `mem_append`.

declarations.name: chainCoeff_reflectionPerm_left_aux
declarations.nl_statement: After reflecting the root indexed by `i` to `-i`, the integer interval `[-chainTopCoeff(i,j), chainBotCoeff(i,j)]` coincides with `[-chainBotCoeff(-i,j), chainTopCoeff(-i,j)]`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Introduce the negation index instance and split on whether `P.root i` and `P.root j` are linearly independent. In the independent case, first transport independence to `P.root (-i)` and `P.root j`. Then prove equality of the two intervals by extensionality in an arbitrary integer `z`: rewrite interval membership using the characterizations of chain coefficients in terms of root expressions lying in the range, simplify the reflected root formulae, and finish with linear arithmetic (`lia`). In the dependent case, all four chain coefficients collapse to their degenerate values, so the interval equality follows by simp.
declarations.divergence: The mathematical idea is clear, but the Lean proof is rewrite-heavy and relies on a large stack of specialized lemmas plus `lia`, so the argument is less transparent than the statement.

declarations.name: chainCoeff_reflectionPerm_right_aux
declarations.nl_statement: Reflecting on the right index `j` similarly sends the interval `[-chainTopCoeff(i,j), chainBotCoeff(i,j)]` to `[-chainBotCoeff(i,-j), chainTopCoeff(i,-j)]`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again split on linear independence of `P.root i` and `P.root j`. In the independent case, transport independence to `P.root i` and `P.root (-j)`, extensionality-reduce interval equality to equivalence of membership for each integer `z`, rewrite membership via the root-chain characterizations, use the formula for the reflected root together with identities converting subtraction to addition and the criterion for negation preserving membership in the root range, and conclude. In the dependent case, simp using the lemmas that chain coefficients are degenerate when independence fails.
declarations.divergence: Same high-level strategy as the left-aux lemma, but even more rewrite-dense; the proof is correct and conceptually motivated, yet Lean presentation is fairly indirect.

declarations.name: chainTopCoeff_reflectionPerm_left
declarations.nl_statement: Reflecting the left root sends the top coefficient of the chain to the original bottom coefficient: `chainTopCoeff (reflectionPerm i i) j = chainBotCoeff i j`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use the auxiliary interval equality from `chainCoeff_reflectionPerm_left_aux` to get, for every integer `z`, equivalent membership in the two relevant intervals. Then compare the endpoints by plugging in the specific endpoint values. One direction comes from inserting `P.chainTopCoeff (-i) j` into the transported interval membership; the other comes from inserting `P.chainBotCoeff i j`. These two endpoint inequalities combine by antisymmetry to yield equality.
declarations.divergence: The proof follows the intended interval-endpoint argument, though the endpoint extraction is encoded via `simpa` on interval membership rather than stated explicitly.

declarations.name: chainBotCoeff_reflectionPerm_left
declarations.nl_statement: Reflecting the left root sends the bottom coefficient of the chain to the original top coefficient: `chainBotCoeff (reflectionPerm i i) j = chainTopCoeff i j`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: As in the previous lemma, start from the interval equality supplied by `chainCoeff_reflectionPerm_left_aux`. Turn it into an equivalence of membership for any integer, then evaluate that equivalence at the negated endpoint values `-P.chainBotCoeff (-i) j` and `-P.chainTopCoeff i j`. The resulting pair of inequalities gives both directions, and antisymmetry concludes the equality of coefficients.
declarations.divergence: Still close to the math, but the use of negated endpoints and interval membership makes the Lean proof slightly less immediately readable.

pr_summary: This PR generalizes several dual-space separation lemmas from free/commutative or field hypotheses to projective/noncommutative settings, chiefly by isolating a projective-module separation lemma and reusing it in quotient arguments.

declarations.name: Module.Projective.exists_dual_ne_zero
declarations.nl_statement: For a projective module V over a semiring R, every nonzero vector x in V is detected by some linear functional f : Dual R V with f x ≠ 0.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use that a projective module splits off a free module: obtain maps i : V → M and s : M → V with s ∘ i = id. Choose a basis b of the free module M. Since x ≠ 0, injectivity of i implies i x ≠ 0. In basis coordinates, b.repr (i x) is a nonzero finitely supported function, so some coordinate j is nonzero. The corresponding coordinate functional b.coord j composed with i is the required dual map on V, and its value at x is exactly that nonzero coordinate.
declarations.divergence: Very direct. The Lean proof follows the standard mathematical argument almost line by line: split projective through a free module, pick a nonzero coordinate in a basis expansion, then compose the coordinate map with the embedding.

declarations.name: Module.forall_dual_apply_eq_zero_iff
declarations.nl_statement: For a projective module V over a semiring R and v : V, all linear functionals vanish on v iff v = 0.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: One direction is immediate by substitution when v = 0. For the converse, argue contrapositively: if v ≠ 0, the projective separation lemma gives a dual functional φ with φ v ≠ 0, contradicting the assumption that every dual functional vanishes on v.
declarations.divergence: Extremely direct. The Lean script is just the biconditional setup, a contraposition step, and an application of `Projective.exists_dual_ne_zero`.

declarations.name: Submodule.exists_dual_map_eq_bot_of_notMem
declarations.nl_statement: Let p be a submodule of an R-module M. If x ∉ p and the quotient M ⧸ p is projective, then there exists a linear functional f : Dual R M such that f x ≠ 0 and p.map f = ⊥.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: First prove the analogous claim on the quotient: since x ∉ p, its class `mkQ x` is nonzero in M ⧸ p. By projectivity of the quotient, some quotient functional detects `mkQ x`. Compose this functional with the quotient map `mkQ : M → M ⧸ p` to obtain a functional on M. Its value on x is still nonzero, and because the functional vanishes on p by factoring through the quotient, the image submodule `p.map f` is bottom; this is discharged by a simp computation with `Submodule.map_comp`.
declarations.divergence: Direct and cleaner than the old proof: it converts `x ∉ p` to nonzero quotient class and then applies the new separation lemma instead of rewriting through a universal vanishing criterion.

declarations.name: Submodule.exists_dual_map_eq_bot_of_lt_top
declarations.nl_statement: If p is a proper submodule of M and the quotient M ⧸ p is projective, then there exists a nonzero linear functional f : Dual R M with p.map f = ⊥.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Choose x outside p using p < ⊤. Apply `exists_dual_map_eq_bot_of_notMem` to get f with f x ≠ 0 and p.map f = ⊥. Since a map taking x to a nonzero value cannot itself be zero, f is nonzero, yielding the result.
declarations.divergence: The proof closely mirrors the mathematical argument. The only mildly indirect part is the first witness extraction from `p < ⊤`, and the nonzeroness of f is closed by `aesop` rather than an explicit sentence.

declarations.name: Submodule.span_eq_top_of_ne_zero
declarations.nl_statement: Assume M is reflexive. If a set s of linear forms has the property that every nonzero z ∈ M is hit nontrivially by some f ∈ s, and the quotient of the dual by `span R s` is projective, then `span R s = ⊤`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Assume for contradiction that `span R s` is proper. By the previous quotient-separation lemma applied to the submodule `span R s` of the dual space, obtain a nonzero dual functional φ on `Dual R M` vanishing on `span R s`. Via reflexivity (`evalEquiv`), regard φ as evaluation at some vector `φs : M`. Every `f ∈ s` lies in the span, so φ(f)=0; translated through `evalEquiv`, this means `f φs = 0` for all `f ∈ s`. Since φ is nonzero, the corresponding vector `φs` is nonzero; applying the hypothesis h to `φs` gives some `f ∈ s` with `f φs ≠ 0`, contradiction.
declarations.divergence: The overall strategy is mathematically natural and the first half is transparent. Some implementation details—especially converting vanishing on the span into `f φs = 0` via `mem_map` and `evalEquiv`—are a bit encoded in library lemmas, so the proof is slightly less immediately readable than the statement.

declarations.name: Module.Dual.range_eq_top_of_ne_zero

declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Apply the standard criterion `LinearMap.range_eq_top` and discharge surjectivity using the existing result that a nonzero linear functional to the scalar ring is surjective over a division semiring.
declarations.divergence: Completely direct: it is a one-line wrapper around existing lemmas expressing exactly the mathematical fact.

pr_summary: This PR simplifies one injectivity proof, adds a weaker equality-based injectivity criterion as `Function.Injective.of_eq_imp_le`, and begins the renaming toward dot-notation-friendly injectivity lemmas.

declarations.name: injective_of_lt_imp_ne

The Lean proof compresses this standard trichotomy argument into `grind [Injective]`.

declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Apply `Meromorphic.prod` to the family, then rewrite the bundled finite product of functions into the explicit pointwise lambda using `Finset.prod_apply`; `simpa` finishes the conversion.
declarations.divergence: Slightly indirect in the same way as `fun_sum`: the proof goes through the function-valued product theorem and then rewrites notation.

declarations.name: Meromorphic.div
declarations.nl_statement: The quotient of two globally meromorphic scalar-valued functions is globally meromorphic.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: At each point `x`, apply the local division closure lemma `MeromorphicAt.div` to `hf x` and `hg x`. This yields local meromorphy of `f / g` everywhere.
declarations.divergence: No divergence: exactly the expected pointwise argument.

declarations.name: Meromorphic.fun_div
declarations.nl_statement: If `f` and `g` are globally meromorphic scalar-valued functions, then `fun x ↦ f x / g x` is globally meromorphic.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Immediate lambda-form restatement of `Meromorphic.div`, proved by reference to that lemma.
declarations.divergence: No substantive divergence; notation only.

declarations.name: Meromorphic.pow
declarations.nl_statement: A natural-number power of a globally meromorphic scalar-valued function is globally meromorphic.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Fix `x`; from `hf x : MeromorphicAt f x`, the local theorem `MeromorphicAt.pow n` yields `MeromorphicAt (f ^ n) x`. Therefore `f ^ n` is globally meromorphic.
declarations.divergence: No divergence: direct pointwise lifting of the local power lemma.

declarations.name: Meromorphic.fun_pow
declarations.nl_statement: If `f` is globally meromorphic, then `fun x ↦ f x ^ n` is globally meromorphic.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is the explicit-lambda version of `Meromorphic.pow`, obtained by direct reuse.
declarations.divergence: No substantive divergence.

declarations.name: Meromorphic.zpow
declarations.nl_statement: An integer power of a globally meromorphic scalar-valued function is globally meromorphic.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: For each point `x`, apply the local lemma `MeromorphicAt.zpow n` to the witness `hf x`. This proves global meromorphy of `f ^ n` for integer `n`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence: straightforward pointwise reuse.

declarations.name: Meromorphic.fun_zpow
declarations.nl_statement: If `f` is globally meromorphic, then `fun x ↦ f x ^ n` for integer `n` is globally meromorphic.

declarations.name: Meromorphic.deriv
declarations.nl_statement: The derivative of a globally meromorphic function is globally meromorphic.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: At each point `x`, the local meromorphicity witness `hf x` can be fed to the existing local theorem `MeromorphicAt.deriv`, giving meromorphy of `deriv f` at `x`. Therefore the derivative is globally meromorphic.
declarations.divergence: No divergence: a direct pointwise application of the local derivative theorem.

declarations.name: Meromorphic.fun_deriv
declarations.nl_statement: If `f` is globally meromorphic, then the explicit pointwise derivative function `fun x ↦ deriv f x` is globally meromorphic.

declarations.name: Meromorphic.iterated_deriv

pr_summary: Adds twelve lemmas identifying `Finset.Ixx` intervals on `Fin n` when one endpoint is shifted by `±1`, all proved by reducing interval membership to inequalities on `Fin.val` and letting `grind` discharge the resulting arithmetic.

declarations.name: Fin.Iio_add_one_eq_Iic
declarations.nl_statement: For `b : Fin n`, assuming `b + 1 < n`, the strict lower interval below `b + 1` equals the closed lower interval up to `b`: `Iio (b + 1) = Iic b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof treats two finsets as equal by extensionality on membership. Membership in `Iio (b + 1)` means `x < b + 1`, while membership in `Iic b` means `x ≤ b`. Expanding `Fin.lt_def` and `Fin.le_def`, and rewriting the value of `b + 1` using `Fin.val_add_one_of_lt'` under the hypothesis `b + 1 < n`, turns the goal into the natural-number equivalence `x.val < b.val + 1 ↔ x.val ≤ b.val`, which `grind` solves.
declarations.divergence: Very low: the Lean proof is essentially the textbook argument, just automated after unfolding the relevant `Fin` comparison and successor-value lemmas.

declarations.name: Fin.Iic_sub_one_eq_Iio
declarations.nl_statement: For nonzero `b : Fin n`, if `0 < b` then the closed lower interval up to `b - 1` equals the strict lower interval below `b`: `Iic (b - 1) = Iio b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again the proof compares membership conditions. After introducing the positivity hypothesis, membership in `Iic (b - 1)` is `x ≤ b - 1`, and membership in `Iio b` is `x < b`. Unfolding `Fin.le_def` and `Fin.lt_def`, and rewriting `(b - 1).val` via `Fin.val_sub_one_of_ne_zero` using the induced `b ≠ 0`, reduces the statement to `x.val ≤ b.val - 1 ↔ x.val < b.val`, which `grind` proves.
declarations.divergence: Low: the proof exactly follows the expected order-theoretic arithmetic reduction, though the use of an implicit `haveI := b.neZero` and `grind` hides some small bookkeeping.

declarations.name: Fin.Ici_add_one_eq_Ioi
declarations.nl_statement: For `a : Fin n`, assuming `a + 1 < n`, the closed upper interval from `a + 1` equals the strict upper interval above `a`: `Ici (a + 1) = Ioi a`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof unfolds membership: `x ∈ Ici (a + 1)` means `a + 1 ≤ x`, and `x ∈ Ioi a` means `a < x`. After expanding `Fin.le_def` and `Fin.lt_def` and rewriting `(a + 1).val` with `Fin.val_add_one_of_lt'`, the goal becomes the natural-number equivalence `a.val + 1 ≤ x.val ↔ a.val < x.val`, which `grind` discharges.
declarations.divergence: Very low: it is the direct arithmetic translation of the statement, packaged into a one-line automation proof.

declarations.name: Fin.Ioi_sub_one_eq_Ici
declarations.nl_statement: For nonzero `a : Fin n`, if `0 < a` then the strict upper interval above `a - 1` equals the closed upper interval from `a`: `Ioi (a - 1) = Ici a`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The equality is proved by rewriting membership predicates. `x ∈ Ioi (a - 1)` means `a - 1 < x`, while `x ∈ Ici a` means `a ≤ x`. Unfolding `Fin.lt_def` and `Fin.le_def` and rewriting `(a - 1).val` as `a.val - 1` using `Fin.val_sub_one_of_ne_zero` turns this into `a.val - 1 < x.val ↔ a.val ≤ x.val`, which `grind` proves from basic arithmetic.
declarations.divergence: Low: the proof is a straightforward reduction to naturals, with only the automation obscuring the explicit extensionality and arithmetic steps.

declarations.name: Fin.Ioc_sub_one_eq_Icc
declarations.nl_statement: For nonzero `a : Fin n`, if `0 < a` then the half-open interval `(a - 1, b]` equals the closed interval `[a, b]`: `Ioc (a - 1) b = Icc a b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Membership in `Ioc (a - 1) b` is the conjunction `a - 1 < x ∧ x ≤ b`, while membership in `Icc a b` is `a ≤ x ∧ x ≤ b`. The right-end condition is unchanged; on the left, unfolding `Fin.lt_def` and `Fin.le_def` and rewriting `(a - 1).val` using `Fin.val_sub_one_of_ne_zero` gives `a.val - 1 < x.val ↔ a.val ≤ x.val`. `grind` then handles the conjunctions and the arithmetic equivalence.
declarations.divergence: Very low: this is exactly the evident interval-membership argument, with automation only compressing routine boolean and arithmetic manipulations.

declarations.name: Fin.Icc_add_one_eq_Ioc
declarations.nl_statement: For `a b : Fin n`, assuming `a + 1 < n`, the closed interval `[a + 1, b]` equals the half-open interval `(a, b]`: `Icc (a + 1) b = Ioc a b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof compares membership conditions `a + 1 ≤ x ∧ x ≤ b` and `a < x ∧ x ≤ b`. After expanding `Fin.le_def` and `Fin.lt_def` and rewriting `(a + 1).val` with `Fin.val_add_one_of_lt'`, the differing left condition becomes `a.val + 1 ≤ x.val ↔ a.val < x.val`; `grind` then solves the entire conjunction equivalence.
declarations.divergence: Very low: the Lean proof mirrors the obvious mathematical equivalence exactly.

declarations.name: Fin.Ioo_sub_one_eq_Ico
declarations.nl_statement: For nonzero `a : Fin n`, if `0 < a` then the open interval `(a - 1, b)` equals the left-closed right-open interval `[a, b)`: `Ioo (a - 1) b = Ico a b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Extensionality reduces the finset equality to `a - 1 < x ∧ x < b ↔ a ≤ x ∧ x < b`. Rewriting `Fin` comparisons in terms of values, and replacing `(a - 1).val` with `a.val - 1` via `Fin.val_sub_one_of_ne_zero`, leaves the arithmetic fact `a.val - 1 < x.val ↔ a.val ≤ x.val`; `grind` finishes.
declarations.divergence: Very low: same direct interval-membership argument as expected, with no conceptual detours.

declarations.name: Fin.Ico_add_one_eq_Ioo
declarations.nl_statement: For `a b : Fin n`, assuming `a + 1 < n`, the interval `[a + 1, b)` equals the open interval `(a, b)`: `Ico (a + 1) b = Ioo a b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Membership is `a + 1 ≤ x ∧ x < b` on the left and `a < x ∧ x < b` on the right. Unfolding `Fin.le_def` and `Fin.lt_def`, rewriting `(a + 1).val`, and reducing to naturals turns the left-side difference into `a.val + 1 ≤ x.val ↔ a.val < x.val`, after which `grind` proves the conjunction equivalence.
declarations.divergence: Very low: it is the standard one-step arithmetic translation of the shifted-endpoint claim.

declarations.name: Fin.Icc_sub_one_eq_Ico
declarations.nl_statement: For nonzero `b : Fin n`, if `0 < b` then the closed interval `[a, b - 1]` equals the right-open interval `[a, b)`: `Icc a (b - 1) = Ico a b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Here the left-end condition `a ≤ x` is unchanged, while the right-end condition changes from `x ≤ b - 1` to `x < b`. Unfolding `Fin.le_def` and `Fin.lt_def` and rewriting `(b - 1).val` using `Fin.val_sub_one_of_ne_zero` reduces the proof to `x.val ≤ b.val - 1 ↔ x.val < b.val`, which `grind` proves inside the conjunction.
declarations.divergence: Very low: the proof is mathematically transparent once one knows the standard `Fin.val` lemmas.

declarations.name: Fin.Ico_add_one_eq_Icc
declarations.nl_statement: For `a b : Fin n`, assuming `b + 1 < n`, the right-open interval `[a, b + 1)` equals the closed interval `[a, b]`: `Ico a (b + 1) = Icc a b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The left condition `a ≤ x` is common to both sides; the only change is `x < b + 1` versus `x ≤ b`. Expanding `Fin` order definitions and rewriting `(b + 1).val` with `Fin.val_add_one_of_lt'` converts this to `x.val < b.val + 1 ↔ x.val ≤ b.val`, which `grind` proves.
declarations.divergence: Very low: the proof follows the exact intended idea with minimal Lean-specific overhead.

declarations.name: Fin.Ioc_sub_one_eq_Ioo
declarations.nl_statement: For nonzero `b : Fin n`, if `0 < b` then the interval `(a, b - 1]` equals the open interval `(a, b)`: `Ioc a (b - 1) = Ioo a b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Membership on the two sides is `a < x ∧ x ≤ b - 1` and `a < x ∧ x < b`. The first conjunct is identical, and the second is transformed by unfolding `Fin.le_def`/`Fin.lt_def` and rewriting `(b - 1).val` via `Fin.val_sub_one_of_ne_zero`, reducing to `x.val ≤ b.val - 1 ↔ x.val < b.val`; `grind` then settles the whole equivalence.

declarations.name: Fin.Ioo_add_one_eq_Ioc
declarations.nl_statement: For `a b : Fin n`, assuming `b + 1 < n`, the open interval `(a, b + 1)` equals the half-open interval `(a, b]`: `Ioo a (b + 1) = Ioc a b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The left condition `a < x` appears on both sides; the only difference is `x < b + 1` versus `x ≤ b`. After unfolding `Fin.lt_def` and `Fin.le_def` and rewriting `(b + 1).val` with `Fin.val_add_one_of_lt'`, the remaining arithmetic equivalence is `x.val < b.val + 1 ↔ x.val ≤ b.val`, which `grind` proves along with the unchanged conjunct.
declarations.divergence: Very low: this is a clean, direct reduction of interval membership to a standard natural-number fact.

pr_summary: This PR rebundles `MonoidAlgebra.mapDomain`/`domCongr` using bundled homomorphisms directly (`M →ₙ* N`, `M →* N`, `M ≃* N`) instead of generic hom-class typeclass arguments, with the resulting proofs mostly inherited from existing ring-level constructions.

declarations.name: MonoidAlgebra.mapDomainNonUnitalAlgHom
declarations.nl_statement: Given a non-unital multiplicative homomorphism `f : M →ₙ* N`, there is a non-unital `R`-algebra homomorphism `A[M] →ₙₐ[R] A[N]` induced by mapping the monoid index of each basis term along `f`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The definition is assembled by reusing the already bundled non-unital ring homomorphism `mapDomainNonUnitalRingHom A f` as the underlying map, then supplying the remaining algebra structure fields directly from existing lemmas: multiplicativity is `mapDomain_mul f`, and compatibility with scalar multiplication is `mapDomain_smul`. So the proof is essentially just packaging previously proved facts under the more specific bundled input type.
declarations.divergence: Very low divergence: the Lean code is almost exactly the mathematical construction 'use the existing ring hom and prove it respects `R`-scalars'.

declarations.name: MonoidAlgebra.mapDomain_algebraMap
declarations.nl_statement: For any monoid hom-class map `f` and scalar `r : k`, applying `mapDomain f` to the image of `r` under the algebra map into `A[G]` gives the image of `r` under the algebra map into `A[H]`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof unfolds the algebra map as `single 1 (algebraMap k A r)` via `coe_algebraMap`, then simplifies `mapDomain` on a singleton using `mapDomain_single` and the fact that a monoid hom sends `1` to `1` (`map_one`). After those rewrites, both sides are definitionally the same, so `simp only` closes the goal.
declarations.divergence: Minimal divergence: it is a direct computation on the explicit formula for the algebra map and `mapDomain`.

declarations.name: MonoidAlgebra.mapDomainAlgHom
declarations.nl_statement: Given a monoid homomorphism `f : M →* N`, there is an `R`-algebra homomorphism `A[M] →ₐ[R] A[N]` induced by mapping indices along `f`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The definition takes the existing ring homomorphism `mapDomainRingHom A f` as the underlying ring map. The only extra algebra-hom field to prove is that scalars commute with the map, and this is discharged by `simp`, which uses the explicit behavior of `mapDomain` on algebra maps (equivalently the previously established `mapDomain_algebraMap`-style simplification). Thus the proof is just bundling the known ring-level map and verifying scalar preservation automatically.
declarations.divergence: Very low divergence: mathematically it says 'the ring hom also preserves the algebra map', and Lean expresses exactly that with one inherited field and one `simp` proof.

declarations.name: MonoidAlgebra.domCongr
declarations.nl_statement: A multiplicative equivalence `e : G ≃* H` induces an `k`-algebra equivalence `A[G] ≃ₐ[k] A[H]` between the corresponding monoid algebras.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The construction uses the existing ring equivalence `mapDomainRingEquiv A e` as the underlying ring equivalence. To upgrade it to an algebra equivalence, it remains only to show that it commutes with the scalar algebra maps. The proof extensionality-reduces the statement to coefficients and then simplifies, using the fact that the ring equivalence acts by relabeling the monoid index and therefore fixes the scalar-supported term at `1`.
declarations.divergence: Low divergence: the proof follows the obvious mathematical route of reusing the ring equivalence and checking scalar compatibility pointwise; the `ext; simp` presentation is concise but still transparent.
