pr_summary: The PR proves that for a continuous function, passing from the whole domain to a dense subset does not change the set of upper/lower bounds of its image, and therefore does not change the corresponding suprema/infima; in linear orders it also handles the unbounded cases automatically.

declarations.name: Dense.continuous_upperBounds
declarations.nl_statement: Let `S` be a dense subset of a topological space `γ`, and let `f : γ → α` be continuous into a preordered space `α` where every lower ray `(-∞, x]` is closed. Then the set of upper bounds of `f(S)` is exactly the set of upper bounds of the full range of `f`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: One inclusion is immediate because `f '' S ⊆ range f`, so any upper bound of the whole range is an upper bound of the smaller image. For the converse, start with an upper bound `x` of `f '' S`. By continuity and density, every value in `range f` lies in the closure of `f '' S`. So it suffices to show that the set `{y | y ≤ x}` is closed and contains `f '' S`; then it also contains the closure, hence all of `range f`. The proof implements exactly this closure argument using `range_subset_closure_image_dense`, rewrites closure membership via `mem_closure_iff_frequently`, and finishes with closedness of `Iic x`.
declarations.divergence: Very close to the standard mathematical proof. The only non-obvious Lean-specific step is proving membership in a closed set from `mem_closure_iff_frequently`, which is a technical encoding of the closure argument rather than a conceptual detour.

declarations.name: Dense.continuous_lowerBounds
declarations.nl_statement: Let `S` be a dense subset of a topological space `γ`, and let `f : γ → α` be continuous into a preordered space `α` where every upper ray `[x, ∞)` is closed. Then the set of lower bounds of `f(S)` is exactly the set of lower bounds of the full range of `f`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is the lower-bound dual of the previous theorem. One inclusion comes from `f '' S ⊆ range f`. For the other, if `x` is a lower bound on `f '' S`, then `f '' S ⊆ Ici x`, and continuity plus density gives `range f ⊆ closure (f '' S)`. Since `Ici x` is closed, it contains the closure as well, so `x` is a lower bound for every value of `f`. Lean follows this plan verbatim, replacing `Iic` by `Ici` and `upperBounds` by `lowerBounds`.
declarations.divergence: Essentially a direct dualization of the previous proof, with no extra ideas beyond the closure-of-image argument.

declarations.name: Dense.continuous_sup
declarations.nl_statement: If `f : γ → α` is continuous into a conditionally complete lattice with closed lower rays, `S ⊆ γ` is dense, and the range of `f` is bounded above, then the supremum of `f` over all of `γ` equals the supremum of `f` over `S`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: First rewrite both indexed suprema as `sSup` of the corresponding ranges. If `γ` is empty, both sides are trivial. Otherwise, the supremum over `range f` is characterized by `isLUB_csSup`. To show the same element is also the supremum over `f '' S`, use `Dense.continuous_upperBounds` to identify the upper-bound sets of the two images, then transfer the `IsLUB` statement across this equality via `isLUB_congr`. The `isLUB_ciSup_set` theorem supplies the `IsLUB` for the subtype-indexed supremum over `S`, and boundedness is restricted from `range f` to the subtype range by a monotonicity lemma discharged by `grind`.
declarations.divergence: The mathematical content is straightforward: equal upper-bound sets imply equal sups. The Lean proof is still short and faithful, but it is mediated through several library characterizations (`sSup_range`, `isLUB_csSup`, `isLUB_ciSup_set`, `isLUB_congr`) and an explicit empty-type split, so it reads more API-driven than the underlying idea.

declarations.name: Dense.continuous_inf
declarations.nl_statement: If `f : γ → α` is continuous into a conditionally complete lattice with closed upper rays, `S ⊆ γ` is dense, and the range of `f` is bounded below, then the infimum of `f` over all of `γ` equals the infimum of `f` over `S`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is the dual argument for infima. Rewrite both infima as `sInf` of the relevant ranges; handle the empty-domain case separately; then use `isGLB_csInf` to characterize the infimum over `range f`. By `Dense.continuous_lowerBounds`, the lower-bound sets of `range f` and `f '' S` coincide, so `isGLB_congr` transfers the greatest-lower-bound statement to the dense-set image. Finally `isGLB_ciInf_set` identifies the subtype-indexed infimum over `S`.
declarations.divergence: Again very close to the conceptual dual proof, though the expression through `csInf`/`IsGLB` lemmas and the subtype boundedness bookkeeping makes it slightly more formal-library-oriented than the plain mathematical argument.

declarations.name: Dense.continuous_sup'
declarations.nl_statement: If `f : γ → α` is continuous into a conditionally complete linear order with closed lower rays and `S` is dense, then the supremum of `f` over all of `γ` equals the supremum of `f` over `S`, without assuming the range is bounded above.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: As before, rewrite both sides as `sSup` of ranges and split off the empty-domain case. Then do a case split on whether `range f` is bounded above. In the bounded case, the previous `IsLUB` argument from `Dense.continuous_sup` works unchanged. In the unbounded case, it is enough to show that the restricted range on the subtype `S` is also unbounded above; otherwise a bound on `f '' S` would, after taking closures and using continuity, yield a bound on `range f`, contradicting the assumption. Lean proves this by identifying the subtype range with `f '' S`, taking the closure of a hypothetical upper-bounded set, pushing it through `image_closure_subset_closure_image hf`, and using density (`closure S = univ`) to conclude the whole range is bounded. Once both sides are known unbounded, both `csSup`s reduce by `csSup_of_not_bddAbove`, so the equality is immediate.
declarations.divergence: The overall math is natural—bounded case by the previous theorem, unbounded case by showing the dense restriction is also unbounded—but the Lean proof of the unbounded transfer is fairly technical. It relies on subtype/range manipulation, closure monotonicity, and image-closure lemmas, so the implementation is less transparent than the underlying argument.

declarations.name: Dense.continuous_inf'
declarations.nl_statement: If `f : γ → α` is continuous into a conditionally complete linear order with closed upper rays and `S` is dense, then the infimum of `f` over all of `γ` equals the infimum of `f` over `S`, without assuming the range is bounded below.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is the dual of `Dense.continuous_sup'`. Rewrite as `sInf` of ranges and split on emptiness of `γ`. If `range f` is bounded below, conclude exactly as in `Dense.continuous_inf`. If not, show the subtype range over `S` is also not bounded below: a lower bound on the dense image would extend to the closure by continuity, and density would force a lower bound on the whole range, contradiction. After this, both conditional infima are evaluated by `csInf_of_not_bddBelow`, giving the claimed equality.
declarations.divergence: Conceptually this is a clean dual proof, but the Lean script inherits the same technical overhead as `continuous_sup'`: subtype range rewrites, closure monotonicity, and image-closure machinery obscure the simplicity of the mathematical idea.

pr_summary: This PR introduces `to_dual` annotations throughout `CategoryTheory.Category.Basic`, so that many right/left dual lemmas and `Mono`/`Epi` infrastructure are generated from one another instead of being maintained separately.

declarations.name: Category.assoc'
declarations.nl_statement: For composable morphisms written in the reversed order, `h ≫ g ≫ f = (h ≫ g) ≫ f`. Equivalently, it is the symmetric form of associativity.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof is exactly `Category.assoc h g f` with both sides swapped via `.symm`. So it directly reuses associativity and does nothing else.
declarations.divergence: None beyond choosing the symmetric orientation explicitly.

declarations.name: eq_whisker
declarations.nl_statement: If `w : f = g`, then postcomposing by any `h` preserves equality: `f ≫ h = g ≫ h`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite by `w`; after replacing `g` by `f` the goal is reflexive.
declarations.divergence: No divergence; the Lean proof is the textbook one-line argument.

declarations.name: eq_of_comp_left_eq
declarations.nl_statement: If `f` and `g` become equal after postcomposition with every morphism out of `Y`, then `f = g`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Apply the hypothesis to `h = 𝟙 Y`, obtaining `f ≫ 𝟙 Y = g ≫ 𝟙 Y`, then simplify both sides using the identity law to conclude `f = g`.
declarations.divergence: Only minor proof-engineering via `convert ... <;> simp` instead of explicitly naming the specialized equality.

declarations.name: eq_of_comp_left_eq'
declarations.nl_statement: If the two postcomposition functions `h ↦ f ≫ h` and `h ↦ g ≫ h` are equal, then `f = g`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Reduce to `eq_of_comp_left_eq` by extracting from the function equality, for each object `Z` and morphism `h : Y ⟶ Z`, the pointwise equality `f ≫ h = g ≫ h` using `congr_fun` twice.
declarations.divergence: Slightly less direct because the mathematical idea is pointwise extensionality, implemented with nested `congr_fun` and `convert`.

declarations.name: id_of_comp_left_id
declarations.nl_statement: If an endomorphism `f : X ⟶ X` acts as a left identity under composition with every outgoing morphism from `X`, then `f = 𝟙 X`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Specialize the hypothesis to `g = 𝟙 X`, giving `f ≫ 𝟙 X = 𝟙 X`, then simplify the left side by the right identity law to obtain `f = 𝟙 X`.
declarations.divergence: Again only the use of `convert`/`simp` compresses the straightforward specialization-and-simplification argument.

declarations.name: comp_ite
declarations.nl_statement: Composition on the left distributes over an `if`: `f ≫ (if P then g else g') = if P then f ≫ g else f ≫ g'`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof is automated by `aesop`; mathematically it is just case-splitting on `P` and simplifying each branch.
declarations.divergence: The intended argument is simple, but the script hides it behind automation rather than an explicit `by_cases P <;> simp`.

declarations.name: comp_dite
declarations.nl_statement: Composition on the left distributes over a dependent `if`: `f ≫ (if h : P then g h else g' h) = if h : P then f ≫ g h else f ≫ g' h`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Solved by `aesop`; conceptually one does a case split on `P` and simplifies the corresponding dependent branches.
declarations.divergence: Same as `comp_ite`, with additional dependent-`if` bookkeeping hidden inside automation.

declarations.name: Mono
declarations.nl_statement: A morphism `f : X ⟶ Y` is mono if every pair `g h : Z ⟶ X` with `g ≫ f = h ≫ f` must be equal.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: There is no proof term beyond the structure field: the declaration packages the standard right-cancellation property as a class. The important change is that it is now declared as the `to_dual` image of `Epi`.
declarations.divergence: No mathematical divergence; the novelty is metaprogramming metadata rather than proof content.

declarations.name: instEpiId
declarations.nl_statement: The identity morphism on any object is an epimorphism.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: To show left cancellation for `𝟙 X`, assume `𝟙 X ≫ g = 𝟙 X ≫ h`; simplifying both sides gives `g = h`. `aesop` carries out this simplification automatically.
declarations.divergence: The proof is the obvious one, though expressed through automation instead of explicit `simpa`.

declarations.name: cancel_epi
declarations.nl_statement: For an epimorphism `f`, the equation `f ≫ g = f ≫ h` is equivalent to `g = h`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: One direction is exactly the defining cancellation property of `Epi`. The converse is obtained by applying `congr_arg` to the map `k ↦ f ≫ k`.
declarations.divergence: Very slight terseness: the second direction is encoded as `congr_arg _` rather than spelling out the function.

declarations.name: cancel_epi_assoc_iff
declarations.nl_statement: If `f` is epi, then `(f ≫ g) ≫ k = (f ≫ h) ≫ l` iff `g ≫ k = h ≫ l`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: For the forward direction, reassociate both sides to `f ≫ (g ≫ k)` and `f ≫ (h ≫ l)`, then cancel `f` using `cancel_epi`. For the reverse direction, start from `g ≫ k = h ≫ l` and reinsert `f` on the left, simplifying by associativity.
declarations.divergence: The Lean proof mirrors the math closely, with `simpa`/`simp only [Category.assoc, p]` doing the reassociation.

declarations.name: cancel_epi_id
declarations.nl_statement: If `f` is epi, then `f ≫ h = f` iff `h = 𝟙 Y`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is a direct specialization of `cancel_epi` where the second right factor is `𝟙 Y`; after converting to that form, simplification proves the equivalence.
declarations.divergence: Only minor compression through `convert cancel_epi f; simp`.

declarations.name: epi_comp
declarations.nl_statement: The composite of two epimorphisms is an epimorphism.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Given `(f ≫ g) ≫ u = (f ≫ g) ≫ v`, first use `cancel_epi_assoc_iff f` to turn this into `g ≫ u = g ≫ v`, then cancel `g` via `cancel_epi g` to conclude `u = v`.
declarations.divergence: No real divergence; the proof is a concise formalization of the standard cancellation argument.

declarations.name: epi_comp'
declarations.nl_statement: If `hf : Epi f` and `hg : Epi g`, then `f ≫ g` is epi.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The theorem simply asks typeclass search to build the instance, which is exactly the previous `epi_comp` instance.
declarations.divergence: Mathematically trivial once the instance exists, but the proof is indirect because it delegates entirely to instance synthesis (`inferInstance`).

declarations.name: epi_of_epi
declarations.nl_statement: If the composite `f ≫ g` is epi, then `g` is epi.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Assume `g ≫ u = g ≫ v`. By associativity this implies `(f ≫ g) ≫ u = (f ≫ g) ≫ v`, so one can cancel the epi `f ≫ g` and deduce `u = v`.
declarations.divergence: Very direct; the only formal packaging is a `simp only [Category.assoc, w]` to build the cancellable equality.

declarations.name: epi_of_epi_fac
declarations.nl_statement: If `h` is epi and `f ≫ g = h`, then `g` is epi.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Substitute `h` by `f ≫ g` using the given factorization equality, then apply `epi_of_epi f g`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence; this is exactly the mathematical reduction by rewriting.

declarations.name: epi_iff_forall_injective
declarations.nl_statement: A morphism `f` is epi iff for every object `Z`, the function sending `g : Y ⟶ Z` to `f ≫ g` is injective.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: If `f` is epi, injectivity of each composition map is exactly `cancel_epi f`. Conversely, if all these maps are injective, then given `f ≫ g = f ≫ h`, apply injectivity for the relevant target object to conclude `g = h`, which is the `Epi` condition.
declarations.divergence: No meaningful divergence; the proof is a compressed but transparent unpacking of definitions.

declarations.name: instEpiOfIsThin
declarations.nl_statement: In a thin category, every morphism is an epimorphism.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: In a thin category every hom-set is a subsingleton, so any two parallel morphisms are equal. Therefore the cancellation conclusion `g = h` holds regardless of the premise, and `Subsingleton.elim` supplies it.
declarations.divergence: None; the Lean proof is exactly the standard subsingleton argument.

pr_summary: Adds a new Lean file formalizing a highly axiomatized Fourier/Galerkin framework for Navier–Stokes on T³ and derives a claimed smoothness theorem `GalerkinLimit.smooth` via short wrapper lemmas around those axioms.

declarations.name: fourier3D_orthogonal
declarations.nl_statement: For Fourier modes `k,k' : Fin 3 → ℤ` on the three-torus, the integral of `fourier3D k` times the conjugate of `fourier3D k'` is `1` when `k = k'` and `0` otherwise.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof first instantiates the assumed one-dimensional orthogonality formula. It rewrites the 3D integrand pointwise as a product over the three coordinates, using the definitions of `fourier3D` and `fourier1D`, `star_prod`, and product-distribution. Then it applies the axiomatized Fubini formula to separate the torus integral into a product of one-dimensional integrals. After replacing each factor by the 1D orthogonality value, it splits on whether `k = k'`. In the equal case, `simp` evaluates the product to `1`. In the unequal case, it extracts a coordinate where the frequencies differ and shows the finite product has a zero factor, hence is `0`.
declarations.divergence: This is one of the more direct proofs in the file: the Lean script tracks the intended mathematics closely. The only mild mismatch is that the substantive analytic input is outsourced to axioms (`fourier_ortho_integral`, `fubini_torus3`), so the proof is really an algebraic packaging of assumed facts rather than a full derivation.

declarations.name: parseval3D
declarations.nl_statement: For a continuous complex-valued function on `T3`, the `L²` norm squared equals the sum of the squared norms of its Fourier coefficients.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof inserts the assumed Fourier inversion formula pointwise into the integrand, turning `‖f x‖²` into the norm square of the Fourier series expansion. After rewriting the integral with this identity, it applies the axiomatized Parseval theorem for the orthonormal Fourier system, with summability provided by another axiom about Fourier coefficients of continuous functions.
declarations.divergence: Very direct: it is exactly 'expand by Fourier inversion, then apply Parseval.' The main caveat is that every analytic step is assumed as an axiom, so the theorem is a thin wrapper around those assumptions rather than a substantial formal proof.

declarations.name: galerkin_energy_bound
declarations.nl_statement: For any `N`, initial datum `u₀`, and nonnegative time `t`, the `L²` norm of the Galerkin approximation at time `t` is bounded by the `L²` norm of `u₀`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof simply unfolds `GalerkinAt` and `GalerkinProjection`, after which both sides are definitionally equal because `GalerkinProjection` ignores both `N` and `t` and is literally the constant-in-time field `u₀`. The result is closed by `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: The Lean proof is perfectly transparent relative to the definitions actually present. The serious divergence is mathematical: the stated 'Galerkin approximation' is defined as just the initial data, so the energy estimate becomes trivial and does not reflect a genuine Navier–Stokes/Galerkin energy argument.

declarations.name: uniform_vorticity_bound
declarations.nl_statement: Given smooth divergence-free initial data and a finite time interval `[0,T]`, there is a constant `C` such that for every Galerkin level `N` and every `t ∈ [0,T]`, the `L∞` norm of the vorticity of the `N`th Galerkin approximation at time `t` is at most `C`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof fixes `s = 3`, notes that `3 > 5/2`, and defines the candidate constant `C = cSobolev s * hsNorm s u₀ * exp (cGronwall s * T * hsNorm s u₀)`. For fixed `N,t`, it rewrites the vorticity expression by unfolding definitions, then chains three inequalities: Sobolev embedding bounds the `L∞` norm of vorticity by an `H^{s-1}` norm; the axiomatized curl estimate bounds that by the `H^s` norm of the velocity; and the axiomatized Gronwall estimate bounds the latter uniformly on `[0,T]`. A final ring normalization identifies the resulting bound with `C`.
declarations.divergence: The proof script follows the intended analytic template cleanly. However, key hypotheses such as divergence-freeness are unused, and all hard estimates are axioms. Also, because the Galerkin flow is definitionally constant in time, the result is not formalizing an actual nontrivial uniform vorticity argument, only composing assumed inequalities.

declarations.name: bkm_coordinate_invariance
declarations.nl_statement: If `Ω(τ) = ω(φ(τ))` for a temporal lifting `φ`, then the BKM integral in physical time up to `T` equals the lifted-time integral `∫₀^{τ_T} Ω(τ) φ'(τ) dτ` whenever `φ(τ_T)=T`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof unfolds the two integral definitions and first rewrites the lifted integrand using the relation `Ω τ = ω (φ τ)`. It then invokes the interval-integral substitution theorem `integral_comp_mul_deriv` with the differentiability and continuity assumptions supplied by the `TemporalLifting` structure and the continuity of `ω`. After rewriting the endpoints using `φ(0)=0` and `φ(τ_T)=T`, it flips the resulting equality to match the desired orientation.
declarations.divergence: This is a straightforward change-of-variables argument and the Lean code mirrors it closely. The only notable gap is that monotonicity/invertibility properties one would normally expect in a reparameterization argument are not used explicitly; instead the proof relies on a library substitution lemma under the stated differentiability hypotheses.

declarations.name: tau_interval_finite
declarations.nl_statement: For a temporal lifting with derivative bounded below by `φ_min > 0`, every positive physical time `T` has a lifted preimage `τ_T` with `φ(τ_T)=T` and `τ_T ≤ T / φ_min`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof obtains some `τ_T` from surjectivity. It then splits into cases. If `τ_T ≤ 0`, the conclusion follows because `T / φ_min` is positive. Otherwise `τ_T > 0`: using the fundamental theorem of calculus, it rewrites `φ τ_T - φ 0` as `∫₀^{τ_T} φ'`. It also rewrites `φ_min * τ_T` as the integral of the constant function `φ_min` over the same interval. Since `φ_min ≤ φ'(x)` everywhere, monotonicity of interval integrals yields `φ_min * τ_T ≤ φ τ_T = T`. Finally it divides by the positive number `φ_min` and performs some ring rearrangements to deduce `τ_T ≤ T / φ_min`.
declarations.divergence: The proof is mathematically recognizable and mostly direct. There is some extra Lean bookkeeping for interval integrals, sign cases, and algebraic rearrangement. More importantly, this lemma is not used later in the file, so the advertised temporal-lifting control does not actually feed into the main theorem.

declarations.name: bkm_finite_anyT
declarations.nl_statement: For smooth divergence-free initial data, each Galerkin approximation has finite BKM integral on any finite interval `[0,T]`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof gets a uniform vorticity bound `C` on `[0,T]` from `uniform_vorticity_bound` and proposes `C*T` as the witness for `BKMFinite`. It packages the pointwise bound for the chosen `N`, then uses monotonicity of the interval integral to compare the vorticity integral with the integral of the constant function `C`. Finally it computes the constant integral as `C*T`.
declarations.divergence: As Lean, this is very clear and direct. As mathematics relative to the file's narrative, it bypasses the preceding temporal-lifting and coordinate-invariance machinery entirely: finiteness is proved just by a uniform bound plus integrability axiom. So the code diverges substantially from the stated story that BKM finiteness comes via coordinate invariance.

declarations.name: VorticityResponse.regularity
declarations.nl_statement: Given a vorticity-response functional `Φ`, viscosity `ν > 0`, and smooth divergence-free initial data `u₀`, there exist velocity and pressure fields `u,p` such that `u` is smooth in spacetime, solves Navier–Stokes, and has initial value `u₀`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof simply chooses `u` to be `GalerkinProjection 1 u₀`, which by definition is just the constant-in-time field equal to `u₀`, and chooses pressure `p = 0`. It obtains `BKMFinite` only on the interval `[0,1]` from `bkm_finite_anyT`, then applies the axiom `bkm_implies_regularity` to conclude `SmoothSpacetime u`. To prove the PDE, it unfolds `spectralNSResidual`, which is defined to be `0`, so `simp` proves the equation immediately. The initial condition is again definitional after extensionality in the vector component.
declarations.divergence: The script is short and readable, but it diverges drastically from the claimed mathematics. The solution is not constructed as a Galerkin limit; it is just the constant field `u₀`. `SolvesNavierStokes` is vacuous because the residual is defined as zero. The role of `Φ` and `ν > 0` is essentially cosmetic, and regularity is imported from an axiom after checking BKM only up to time `1`, not globally.

declarations.name: GalerkinLimit.smooth
declarations.nl_statement: For any viscosity `ν > 0` and smooth divergence-free initial data on `T3`, there exists a smooth spacetime solution of the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with that initial data.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof defines a specific `VorticityResponse` with bounds `φ_min = 1` and `φ_max = 2`, verifying the required positivity and ordering by elementary inequalities. It then applies `VorticityResponse.regularity` with this chosen structure to obtain the desired existence, smoothness, equation, and initial-value properties.
declarations.divergence: As a Lean wrapper around the preceding theorem, it is perfectly straightforward. But the substantive divergence is inherited wholesale from `VorticityResponse.regularity`: the theorem's impressive statement rests on axioms, vacuous definitions, and a trivial constant solution construction rather than a formalized Galerkin-limit argument.

pr_summary: This PR adds `to_dual` annotations so several predecessor lemmas/instances are now auto-generated from successor-side proofs, with two proof adjustments replacing `succ_mono`/`pred_mono` by dualizable lemmas `succ_le_succ`/`pred_le_pred`.

declarations.name: Order.succ_top
declarations.nl_statement: In an order with a top element, the successor of `⊤` is `⊤`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite `succ (⊤) = ⊤` using the characterization `succ a = a ↔ IsMax a`, then rewrite `IsMax ⊤` as `⊤ = ⊤` via `isMax_iff_eq_top`; the goal becomes immediate by simplification.
declarations.divergence: The Lean proof is exactly the mathematical argument: two rewrites by standard characterizations.

declarations.name: Order.succ_le_iff_eq_top
declarations.nl_statement: In an order with top, `succ a ≤ a` iff `a = ⊤`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use the existing equivalence `succ a ≤ a ↔ IsMax a`, then compose it with `IsMax a ↔ a = ⊤`.
declarations.divergence: Completely direct: the proof is literally the transitive composition of the two iff lemmas.

declarations.name: Order.lt_succ_iff_ne_top
declarations.nl_statement: In an order with top, `a < succ a` iff `a ≠ ⊤`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Start from the standard characterization `a < succ a ↔ ¬ IsMax a`, and then rewrite `¬ IsMax a` as `a ≠ ⊤` using `not_isMax_iff_ne_top`.
declarations.divergence: Again almost verbatim mathematics; Lean just chains two equivalences with `.trans`.

declarations.name: Order.bot_lt_succ
declarations.nl_statement: In a nontrivial order with bottom, the bottom element is strictly below `succ a` for every `a`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: First, since `⊥` is not maximal in a nontrivial order, `⊥ < succ ⊥`. Then use monotonicity of successor in the form `succ ⊥ ≤ succ a`, obtained from `bot_le`, and compose strict-with-weak transitivity to get `⊥ < succ a`.
declarations.divergence: Still straightforward, but the Lean term is a compact composition `(...).trans_le <| succ_le_succ bot_le`; one must recognize that the first fact is applied at `⊥` and the second compares successors.

declarations.name: Order.succ_ne_bot
declarations.nl_statement: In a nontrivial order with bottom, `succ a` is never `⊥`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use the previous theorem `⊥ < succ a`; anything strictly above `⊥` cannot equal `⊥`.
declarations.divergence: Maximally direct one-line extraction of inequality from strict inequality.

declarations.name: Order.lt_succ_bot_iff
declarations.nl_statement: In a linear order with bottom and no maximal element, `a < succ ⊥` iff `a = ⊥`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite `a < succ ⊥` using the no-max-order formula `lt_succ_iff`, which gives `a ≤ ⊥`; then rewrite `a ≤ ⊥` as `a = ⊥`.
declarations.divergence: Pure rewriting, matching the intended argument exactly.

declarations.name: Order.le_succ_bot_iff
declarations.nl_statement: In a linear order with bottom, `a ≤ succ ⊥` iff `a = ⊥` or `a = succ ⊥`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Apply the general linear-order description `a ≤ succ b ↔ a = succ b ∨ a ≤ b` at `b = ⊥`, rewrite `a ≤ ⊥` to `a = ⊥`, and swap the disjuncts to match the stated order.
declarations.divergence: Very direct; only a final `or_comm` reorders the conclusion.

declarations.name: Order.le_succ_pred
declarations.nl_statement: For any element `a` in a preorder with successor and predecessor, `a ≤ succ (pred a)`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The weak cover relation `pred_wcovBy a : pred a ⩿ a` says that `a` lies at or just above `pred a`; its `le_succ` consequence is exactly `a ≤ succ (pred a)`.
declarations.divergence: Direct once one knows the API of weak covers; the proof is a projection from an already-packaged lemma rather than a fresh argument.

declarations.name: Order.pred_le_iff_le_succ
declarations.nl_statement: In a preorder with both predecessor and successor, `pred a ≤ b` iff `a ≤ succ b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: For the forward direction, from `pred a ≤ b`, apply successor monotonicity in the dualizable form `succ_le_succ` to get `succ (pred a) ≤ succ b`, and compose with `a ≤ succ (pred a)`. For the reverse direction, from `a ≤ succ b`, apply predecessor monotonicity `pred_le_pred` to get `pred a ≤ pred (succ b)`, then use `pred (succ b) ≤ b`.
declarations.divergence: The proof follows the standard adjunction pattern closely. The only mild opacity is that both directions are expressed through previously named helper lemmas (`le_succ_pred`, `succ_le_succ`, `pred_le_pred`, `pred_succ_le`) rather than expanded.

declarations.name: WithTop.instIsEmptyPredOrderWithTop
declarations.nl_statement: If `α` is a nonempty preorder with no maximal element, then `WithTop α` cannot carry a `PredOrder` structure.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Assume such a predecessor structure on `WithTop α`. Inspect `pred ⊤`. If `pred ⊤ = ⊤`, then choose some `a : α`; the predecessor axiom `min_of_le_pred` would force `⊤` to be minimal, contradicting `a < ⊤`. If `pred ⊤ = a` for some `a : α`, use no-maximality to pick `c > a`; transporting this to `WithTop α`, the axiom `le_pred_of_lt` applied to `c < ⊤` yields `c ≤ pred ⊤ = a`, contradicting `a < c`. Hence no `PredOrder (WithTop α)` exists.
declarations.divergence: The case split mirrors the math, but the Lean proof is somewhat compressed and depends on the exact constructors of `WithTop` plus order-theoretic contradiction lemmas like `.not_lt`/`.not_gt`.

declarations.name: WithBot.instSuccOrderWithBot
declarations.nl_statement: If `α` is a preorder with bottom and successor order, then `WithBot α` inherits a `SuccOrder` by sending the new bottom to itself and every old element to the coercion of its successor.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Define `succ` by cases: `succ ⊥ = ⊥`, and `succ (a : α) = succ a` inside `WithBot`. Then verify the `SuccOrder` axioms case-by-case. For `le_succ`, it is trivial at bottom and reduces to the original axiom on coerced elements. For `max_of_succ_le`, the bottom case is impossible since no coerced element is below bottom; for a coerced element it reduces to the corresponding axiom in `α` and then lifts back. For `succ_le_of_lt`, all mixed cases are either impossible or trivial, and the genuine `α`-case is inherited from `α`.
declarations.divergence: The implementation is the expected case split, but the Lean proof is bookkeeping-heavy because it must analyze `Option` cases and shuttle inequalities through `coe_le_coe`/`coe_lt_coe`.

declarations.name: WithBot.instPredOrderWithBot
declarations.nl_statement: If `α` is a partial order with predecessor order and decidable fixed points of `pred`, then `WithBot α` inherits a `PredOrder`: the new bottom is fixed, and a coerced element drops to bottom exactly when it was already minimal, otherwise to the coercion of its predecessor.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Define `pred` by cases: `pred ⊥ = ⊥`; for `a : α`, set `pred a` to `⊥` if `pred a = a`, otherwise to the coercion of `pred a`. For `pred_le`, check bottom trivially and on coerced elements split on whether `pred a = a`; either the result is bottom or the original `pred_le` lifts through coercion. For `min_of_le_pred`, the bottom case is immediate; on a coerced element, split on `pred a = a`: if so, the assumed inequality would force a coercion below bottom, impossible; otherwise rewrite the inequality via `le_pred_iff_isMin` and `pred_eq_iff_isMin` to contradict the branch assumption. For `le_pred_of_lt`, bottom/coe mixed cases are trivial or impossible, while in the coe/coe case one splits on whether `pred b = b`; if yes, then `b` is minimal and cannot have something strictly below it, contradiction; if not, lift the original `le_pred_of_lt`.
declarations.divergence: Mathematically natural, but the Lean proof is the least transparent of the changed items because it intertwines the case split defining `pred` with multiple impossible `WithBot` cases and branch-specific rewrites from equality-to-minimality characterizations.

pr_summary: This PR only fixes documentation/comments and notation typos across MeasureTheory files; it does not change any non-trivial declaration bodies or proofs.

This PR extends `@[to_fun]` so that hovering over the `to_fun` attribute site shows the generated `fun_...` declaration, by adding an optional `hoverInfo` mode to `addRelatedDecl` and enabling it for `to_fun`.

declarations.name: Mathlib.Tactic.addRelatedDecl
declarations.nl_statement: `addRelatedDecl` builds and registers a new declaration related to an existing declaration `src`, carrying over ranges, protection, doc strings, and selected attributes; the change in this PR adds an optional boolean parameter `hoverInfo` which, when true, attaches term info at the user syntax `ref` so hover on that syntax displays the generated target declaration.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is not a theorem but a meta-program. It computes the target name from `src`, records declaration ranges, fetches the source constant info, asks the caller-supplied `construct` function for the new value and universe parameters, infers the new type, and re-declares the result as a theorem or definition according to the source and the propositionhood of the new type. Afterwards it preserves `protected`, transfers/combines doc strings, infers the reducibility attribute, elaborates and applies any copied attributes to both declarations, and finally, in the new branch introduced by the PR, if `hoverInfo` is true it calls `Term.addTermInfo' ref (← mkConstWithLevelParams tgt) (isBinder := true)`, which is exactly the mechanism that makes hover at `ref` present the generated declaration.
declarations.divergence: The implementation is very direct: the new behavior is a single final conditional side effect added after the existing declaration-generation pipeline. The only mildly non-obvious part is the use of `isBinder := true`, which is a Lean elaboration detail rather than something explained by the surrounding prose.

declarations.name: to_fun
declarations.nl_statement: The builtin attribute `@[to_fun]` creates a new declaration `fun_<src>` by eta-expanding point-free functions in the type of the annotated declaration; the PR changes its registration so that the generated declaration is also used as hover information at the `to_fun` syntax.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again this is meta-code, not a proof. The attribute parser matches `to_fun` with optional copied attributes, checks that it is used globally, and then delegates all declaration creation to `addRelatedDecl`. The constructor it passes infers the type of the source constant, runs `Push.pullCore .lambda` on that type to eta-expand into explicit `fun`-form, errors if nothing changed, and otherwise casts the original value to the transformed type. The PR's behavioral change is simply that this call now sets `(hoverInfo := true)`, so once `addRelatedDecl` has created `fun_<src>`, hover on the original `to_fun` token shows that generated constant.
declarations.divergence: Extremely direct: the implementation matches the intended feature almost literally by flipping on the new `hoverInfo` option in the existing helper call. The only indirect part is that the hover behavior is realized in `addRelatedDecl`, not locally here.

pr_summary: This PR equips the product category of a family of monoidal, braided, symmetric, and closed monoidal categories with the corresponding pointwise structures, and adds the helper `Pi.isoMk` for assembling componentwise isomorphisms.

declarations.name: CategoryTheory.Pi.isoMk

declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The definition simply packages the componentwise `hom` and `inv` maps into a family-valued morphism. The inverse laws are not proved here explicitly because they are discharged by the structure fields inherited for isomorphisms of functions/components.

pr_summary: Adds two polynomial extensionality lemmas saying that over an integral domain, two polynomials are equal if they agree on sufficiently many distinct points, together with a Finset-specialized version.

declarations.name: eq_of_natDegree_lt_card_of_eval_eq
declarations.nl_statement: For polynomials p and q over a commutative domain, if they have the same values on all points f i of a finite family of pairwise distinct evaluation points, and the size of that family is strictly larger than both natDegrees, then p = q.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite the goal p = q as p - q = 0. Apply the previously established lemma saying a polynomial is zero if it vanishes on enough distinct points. For the vanishing hypothesis, use eval (f i) (p - q) = eval (f i) p - eval (f i) q, so the assumption that the evaluations of p and q agree gives zero; this is discharged by `simpa [sub_eq_zero]`. For the degree bound, use the standard inequality natDegree (p - q) ≤ max (natDegree p) (natDegree q), and conclude with the assumed cardinality inequality; Lean packages this last step into `grind [natDegree_sub_le]`.
declarations.divergence: Very direct mathematically: subtract and reduce to the zero-polynomial lemma. The only slight opacity is that the evaluation-to-zero step is hidden behind `simpa [sub_eq_zero]`, and the degree comparison is compressed into `grind [natDegree_sub_le]` rather than written as an explicit chain.

declarations.name: eq_of_natDegree_lt_card_of_eval_eq'
declarations.nl_statement: For polynomials p and q over a commutative domain, if they agree on every element of a finite set s and max p.natDegree q.natDegree is less than the cardinality of s, then p = q.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Specialize the previous lemma to the finite type consisting of elements of the Finset s. The evaluation points are given by the coercion `Subtype.val : s → R`, which is injective, and the pointwise equality hypothesis is obtained by feeding each subtype element i its membership proof i.prop. Finally, convert the cardinality assumption from `#s` to `Fintype.card s` using `Fintype.card_coe s`.
declarations.divergence: This is a transparent wrapper around the previous lemma. It follows the intended specialization exactly, with only the routine cardinality coercion `hcard.trans_eq (Fintype.card_coe s).symm` inserted for Lean.

pr_summary: This PR adds basic monoidal/product infrastructure for truncated simplicial sets and proves several foundational lemmas showing how edges, composition data, and homotopy categories interact with binary products, including a terminality criterion for certain homotopy categories.

declarations.name: SSet.Truncated.Edge.CompStruct.idCompId
declarations.nl_statement: For any vertex `x` of a 2-truncated simplicial set, the identity edge on `x` admits a composition structure as the composite of the identity edge with itself.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The declaration is just a wrapper around the existing lemma `idComp`, specialized to the identity edge. The proof is literally `idComp _`, so the mathematical content is inherited entirely from the earlier construction.
declarations.divergence: None; the Lean term is exactly the intended specialization.

declarations.name: SSet.Truncated.Edge.tensor
declarations.nl_statement: Given edges `e₁ : x ⟶ x'` in `X` and `e₂ : y ⟶ y'` in `Y`, there is an induced edge in the product simplicial set `X ⊗ Y` from `(x,y)` to `(x',y')`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The edge is defined componentwise: take the pair of underlying 1-simplices `(e₁.edge, e₂.edge)` in the product functor, and verify source and target identities by pairing the corresponding equalities for `e₁` and `e₂` with `Prod.ext`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence; this is the direct coordinatewise construction.

declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Starting with an edge `e` in the product, project it along `fst` and `snd` to obtain edges in each factor. Then reconstruct the original edge as the tensor of these projections; this is definitional, so the witness equation is `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: None; the proof follows the obvious projection-reconstruction argument exactly.

declarations.name: SSet.Truncated.Edge.id_tensor_id

declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Both sides reduce to the same componentwise record, so the proof is by reflexivity.
declarations.divergence: None.

declarations.name: SSet.Truncated.Edge.map_tensorHom

declarations.nl_proof_sketch: All constructions involved are componentwise on the underlying product, so both sides are definitionally identical; the proof is `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: None.

declarations.divergence: None.

On one side, use `idComp ex` together with `compId ey`; on the other, `compId ex` with `idComp ey`. Both composites reduce to the same diagonal edge in the product, so rewriting by these two composition lemmas proves the equality.

declarations.name: SSet.Truncated.HomotopyCategory.subsingleton_hom
declarations.nl_statement: If a 2-truncated simplicial set has a unique vertex and at most one edge, then every hom-set in its homotopy category is a subsingleton.

Show `P` is multiplicative: identities belong because every object equals `mk x₀`, and compositions of the unique listed morphisms are still that morphism. Then prove `P = ⊤` via `morphismProperty_eq_top`: any generating edge must be the identity edge, since both endpoints equal `x₀` and the 1-simplex type is subsingleton. Hence every morphism lies in `P`, so any two morphisms are forced to be the unique inhabitant of `P`, giving equality.
declarations.divergence: Noticeable divergence from the shortest mathematical argument. On paper one would say 'there is only one object and only one generating edge, hence only one morphism'; Lean packages this through the existing machinery of multiplicative morphism properties and closure by generators.

pr_summary: This PR redefines `Rat.intEquiv` as the composite of the canonical equivalence from an integral closure to the ring of integers with `Rat.ringOfIntegersEquiv`, and adds a simp lemma showing these coincide when `R = 𝓞 ℚ`.

declarations.name: Rat.intEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: If `R` is a commutative ring with an algebra structure over `ℚ`, is the fraction ring of `ℚ`, and is the integral closure of `ℤ` in `ℚ`, then `R` is canonically ring-isomorphic to `ℤ`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The new definition does not prove bijectivity directly. Instead, it uses the already existing canonical equivalence `NumberField.RingOfIntegers.equiv R : 𝓞 ℚ ≃+* R`, inverts it to get `R ≃+* 𝓞 ℚ`, and then composes with the canonical rational ring-of-integers equivalence `Rat.ringOfIntegersEquiv : 𝓞 ℚ ≃+* ℤ`. Thus the map is obtained by transporting through the ring of integers of `ℚ`.
declarations.divergence: Very direct: the Lean term is exactly the intended mathematical composition, with essentially no proof engineering beyond writing the composite.

declarations.name: Rat.intEquiv_apply_eq_ringOfIntegersEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: For `x : 𝓞 ℚ`, the newly defined `Rat.intEquiv (𝓞 ℚ)` sends `x` to exactly the same integer as `Rat.ringOfIntegersEquiv` does.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof unfolds the definitions of `Rat.intEquiv`, `RingOfIntegers.equiv`, `IsIntegralClosure.equiv`, `IsIntegralClosure.lift`, and `IsIntegralClosure.mk'`, then lets `simp` evaluate the composite. Conceptually, when `R = 𝓞 ℚ`, the first factor in the composite is the identity equivalence on `𝓞 ℚ`, so the whole map reduces to `ringOfIntegersEquiv`.
declarations.divergence: Mathematically the argument is straightforward, but the Lean proof works by aggressively unfolding several implementation-level definitions of integral-closure equivalences and then simplifying, so it is somewhat more tied to library internals than the high-level idea suggests.

pr_summary: This PR adds a new file defining indecomposable elements in a family of monoid elements, proves that this notion recovers irreducibility for the identity family, and formalizes Serre’s lemma that the submonoid generated by all elements with `1 < f (v i)` is already generated by the indecomposable ones among them.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable
declarations.nl_statement: For a family `v : ι → M`, a set of indices `s`, and an index `i`, the predicate `IsMulIndecomposable v s i` means that `i` lies in `s` and whenever `v i` is written as `v j * v k` with `j,k ∈ s`, one of the two factors is trivial, i.e. equal to `1`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is a definition, not a proof. It packages membership in `s` together with the universal factorization condition restricted to indices in `s`.
declarations.divergence: None: the Lean code is just the direct formal definition of the mathematical notion.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable_id_univ
declarations.nl_statement: If the unit group of `M` is subsingleton and `x ≠ 1`, then `x` is indecomposable in the identity family over all of `M` exactly when `x` is irreducible.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The forward direction builds an `Irreducible x`: non-unitness follows from `x ≠ 1` because in a monoid with subsingleton units, being a unit is equivalent to being `1`; the factorization condition is exactly the indecomposability condition specialized to `id` and `univ`, again converting `IsUnit a ∨ IsUnit b` into `a = 1 ∨ b = 1` by `simp`. For the reverse direction, from irreducibility one uses `h.isUnit_or_isUnit` and the same simplification to get the required `= 1` conclusion, while membership in `univ` is trivial.
declarations.divergence: Very small. The proof is compressed into a one-liner using `simpa`, so the structure is slightly implicit, but it matches the standard equivalence almost exactly.

declarations.name: Submonoid.closure_image_one_lt_and_isMulIndecomposable
declarations.nl_statement: Assume `ι` is finite. Let `v : ι → M` be a family in a monoid and `f : M →* S` a monoid homomorphism into a linearly ordered cancel commutative monoid `S`. Then the submonoid generated by those `v i` with `1 < f (v i)` is equal to the submonoid generated by the subfamily of such `v i` that are indecomposable relative to that same set.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: One inclusion is immediate because indecomposable indices with `1 < f (v i)` form a subset of all indices with `1 < f (v i)`. For the reverse inclusion, fix an element `v i` with `1 < f (v i)` and suppose it is not in the closure generated by indecomposables. Let `t` be the set of indecomposable indices and let `s` be the set of indices with `1 < f (v j)` whose values are not in `closure (v '' t)`. This set is nonempty, so by finiteness choose `i ∈ s` minimizing `f (v i)`. By minimality, any `k` with `1 < f (v k) < f (v i)` must already satisfy `v k ∈ closure (v '' t)`. Since `i ∉ t`, `v i` is not indecomposable, so there exist `j,k` with `1 < f (v j)`, `1 < f (v k)`, and `v i = v j * v k`. Because `1 < f (v j)` and `1 < f (v k)`, multiplicativity gives `1 < f (v j), f (v k) < f (v i)`; thus by minimality both `v j` and `v k` lie in the closure. Since the closure is a submonoid, their product `v i` also lies in the closure, contradicting the choice of `i`. Hence every generator with `1 < f (v i)` lies in the closure generated by indecomposables.
declarations.divergence: The overall proof follows the textbook minimal-counterexample argument quite closely. The main compression points are the `grind [IsMulIndecomposable]` step producing the nontrivial factorization from `i ∉ t`, and the `aesop` steps showing `f (v j), f (v k) < f (v i)` from `1 < f (v j)`, `1 < f (v k)`, and `f (v i) = f (v j) * f (v k)`. These automated steps hide some ordered-monoid arithmetic, but the proof skeleton remains faithful to the mathematical argument.

pr_summary: The PR adds convenient self-adjointness lemmas for the Fourier transform on Schwartz space and proves that the Fourier transform and inverse Fourier transform on tempered distributions agree with the classical transforms when a Schwartz function is viewed as a tempered distribution.

declarations.name: integral_fourier_smul_eq
declarations.nl_statement: For a complex-valued Schwartz function f and an F-valued Schwartz function g, the integral of (𝓕 f) acting by scalar multiplication on g equals the integral of f acting by scalar multiplication on 𝓕 g.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is obtained immediately from the more general bilinear self-adjointness theorem `integral_bilin_fourier_eq` by instantiating the bilinear map M with the continuous linear map implementing scalar multiplication, `ContinuousLinearMap.lsmul ℂ ℂ`. No further proof steps are needed.
declarations.divergence: Essentially none: the Lean proof is exactly the mathematical specialization of the general bilinear statement to scalar multiplication.

declarations.name: integral_fourier_mul_eq
declarations.nl_statement: For complex-valued Schwartz functions f and g, the integral of (𝓕 f)·g equals the integral of f·(𝓕 g).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again this is a direct specialization of `integral_bilin_fourier_eq`, this time taking the bilinear form M to be complex multiplication, encoded as `ContinuousLinearMap.mul ℂ ℂ`. The theorem is then exactly the desired identity.
declarations.divergence: None beyond packaging multiplication as a continuous bilinear map.

declarations.name: fourierTransform_toTemperedDistributionCLM_eq
declarations.nl_statement: If a Schwartz function f is regarded as a tempered distribution, then its distributional Fourier transform is exactly the classical Fourier transform of f.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: To prove equality of tempered distributions, the proof extensionality-reduces to testing against an arbitrary Schwartz function g. Evaluating the left-hand side on g gives the pairing of f with 𝓕 g by definition of the distributional Fourier transform, while evaluating the right-hand side gives the pairing with 𝓕 f. The needed equality of these pairings is precisely the previously proved self-adjointness formula `integral_fourier_smul_eq g f`; `simpa` matches the coercions and pairing conventions.
declarations.divergence: Very small: one must recognize that `ext g` unfolds equality of tempered distributions into equality of their actions on test functions, and `simpa` hides the coercion from Schwartz functions to tempered distributions.

declarations.name: fourierTransformInv_toTemperedDistributionCLM_eq
declarations.nl_statement: If a Schwartz function f is viewed as a tempered distribution, then its distributional inverse Fourier transform is exactly the classical inverse Fourier transform of f.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof derives the inverse-transform compatibility from the already established forward-transform compatibility and the fact that Fourier transform and inverse Fourier transform are mutual inverses on both Schwartz functions and tempered distributions. It rewrites f as `𝓕 (𝓕⁻ f)` using `fourier_fourierInv_eq` on Schwartz space, applies the inverse Fourier transform to both sides, then replaces the tempered-distribution image of `𝓕 (𝓕⁻ f)` by the Fourier transform of the tempered-distribution image of `𝓕⁻ f` via `fourierTransform_toTemperedDistributionCLM_eq`, and finally cancels `𝓕⁻ ∘ 𝓕` on tempered distributions using `fourierInv_fourier_eq`.
declarations.divergence: Moderate: the mathematics is standard, but the Lean proof is an algebraic `calc` chain with coercion management (`toTemperedDistributionCLM ...`) and uses inverse laws indirectly rather than unfolding the pairing definition directly.

declarations.nl_statement: A continuous semilinear equivalence e restricts to a continuous semilinear equivalence between a submodule p and its image `p.map e`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Take the underlying linear equivalence to be the existing algebraic `LinearEquiv.submoduleMap`. For continuity of the forward map, view it as the codomain restriction of the composite of e with the subtype inclusion of p, and apply continuity of continuous linear maps. For the inverse, start from continuity of `e.symm`, restrict it to points lying in the image submodule, and use the algebraic inverse to certify that the values land back in p.
declarations.divergence: This follows the natural construction closely, though the proof of continuity of the inverse is expressed via `restrict` and a membership witness extracted from the algebraic inverse, which is slightly more implementation-driven than the mathematical summary.

pr_summary: This PR adds API expressing presieves and sieves as generated by their arrow categories, characterizes sheafness for `ofArrows` covers as bijectivity of the obvious restriction map, and derives invariance/results for `IsSheafFor` under isomorphisms, sieve pullback along isos, and `Over.map`.

declarations.name: Presieve.ofArrows_category
declarations.nl_statement: Any presieve `R` is exactly the presieve obtained by taking as indices the objects of `R.category` and as arrows their underlying morphisms into the base.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof is just extensionality by two inclusions. If an arrow belongs to `Presieve.ofArrows` from `R.category`, it is represented by some object of `R.category`, whose membership proof is precisely the needed proof that the arrow lies in `R`. Conversely, if `g` lies in `R`, package `g` together with its proof as an object of `R.category`; this object gives an index witnessing that `g` is in the `ofArrows` presieve.
declarations.divergence: Virtually none: the Lean proof is the direct set-theoretic argument.

declarations.name: Sieve.ofArrows_category'
declarations.nl_statement: For a presieve `R`, the sieve generated by the family of arrows coming from `R.category` is the same as the sieve `generate R`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again prove equality by two inclusions. For the forward direction, use `Sieve.generate_le_iff` to reduce membership in the generated sieve to checking the generating arrows, and each generator from `R.category` is immediately in `generate R` by taking the identity factorization. For the reverse direction, an element of `generate R` is by definition a factorization through some `b : Y ⟶ S` with `R b`; this `b` is an object of `R.category`, and the same factorization witnesses membership in the sieve generated by those category arrows.
declarations.divergence: Very small; the only abstraction is using `generate_le_iff` to package one inclusion.

declarations.name: Sieve.ofArrows_category
declarations.nl_statement: Any sieve `R` is exactly the sieve generated by the underlying arrows of its arrow category `R.arrows.category`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Reduce immediately to the previous lemma with the underlying presieve `R.arrows`, then use `generate_sieve` to identify `generate R` with `R` itself.
declarations.divergence: None; it is a one-line mathematical rewrite.

declarations.name: Sieve.exists_eq_ofArrows
declarations.nl_statement: Every sieve can be presented as `Sieve.ofArrows _ f` for some indexing type, domains, and family of arrows.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Take the indexing type to be `R.arrows.category`, the domains and arrows given by its objects, and use `Sieve.ofArrows_category` to obtain the desired equality.
declarations.divergence: None; it is exactly the canonical presentation lemma.

declarations.name: Sieve.pullback_ofArrows_of_iso
declarations.nl_statement: Pulling back a sieve generated by arrows `f i : Z i ⟶ X` along an isomorphism `e.hom : X' ⟶ X` gives the sieve generated by the composites `f i ≫ e.inv : Z i ⟶ X'`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Extensionality on arrows into `X'`. An arrow in the pullback means its composite with `e.hom` lies in the original `ofArrows` sieve, so it factors through some `f i`; rewrite that factorization across the isomorphism to show it factors through `f i ≫ e.inv`. Conversely, if an arrow factors through some `f i ≫ e.inv`, then composing with `e.hom` gives a factorization through `f i`, hence membership in the pullback. The Lean proof unpacks the existential witnesses on each side and closes the algebra with `simp`.
declarations.divergence: Low; the proof is the expected bidirectional factorization argument, with only minor bookkeeping around the factorization equality.

declarations.name: isSheafFor_iff_of_iso
declarations.nl_statement: If presheaves `P` and `P'` are isomorphic, then `P` is a sheaf for `R` iff `P'` is a sheaf for `R`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Apply the existing lemma `isSheafFor_iso` in both directions, once with the given isomorphism and once with its inverse.
declarations.divergence: None; this is exactly the obvious equivalence.

declarations.name: Arrows.toCompatible
declarations.nl_statement: Given a section `s` of `P` over `B`, produce the compatible family on the cover arrows `π i : X i ⟶ B` by restricting `s` along each `π i`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Define the family by `i ↦ P.map (π i).op s`. Compatibility follows from functoriality: if `gi ≫ π i = gj ≫ π j`, then the two pullbacks of `s` along those composites agree because they are the same morphism after taking opposites and applying `P.map`. Lean proves this with a one-line `simp` using functoriality of `map` and the equality `h`.
declarations.divergence: Tiny; only the routine `simp`/`dsimp` layer separates the code from the mathematical definition.

declarations.name: isSheafFor_ofArrows_iff_bijective_toCompabible
declarations.nl_statement: For a presheaf of types and an `ofArrows` presieve, the sheaf condition is equivalent to the map sending a section over the target to its induced compatible family on the covering arrows being bijective.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Start from the earlier explicit characterization `isSheafFor_arrows_iff`, which says every compatible family has a unique amalgamation. From this, injectivity of `Arrows.toCompatible` is exactly uniqueness of amalgamations for the compatible family arising from a section, while surjectivity says every compatible family comes from some amalgamation. Conversely, if the map is bijective, then for a compatible family `x`, surjectivity gives a section `y` whose associated family equals `x`; after unpacking the subtype equality, this gives existence, and injectivity shows uniqueness of any two amalgamating sections because they induce the same compatible family. The proof mirrors this plan, though it uses some subtype extensionality and congruence lemmas to pass between equalities of subtype elements and equalities of their underlying families.
declarations.divergence: Moderate but still clear: the core idea is direct, but the Lean proof spends noticeable effort on `Subtype.ext`, `congr_arg Subtype.val`, and rewriting the surjectivity witness.

declarations.name: isSheafFor_pullback_iff
declarations.nl_statement: If `f : Y ⟶ X` is an isomorphism, then a presheaf is a sheaf for the pullback of a sieve `R` along `f` iff it is a sheaf for `R` itself.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: First write `R` as an `ofArrows` sieve using `R.exists_eq_ofArrows`. Then identify the pullback sieve with an `ofArrows` sieve whose arrows are the original ones postcomposed with `inv f`, using `Sieve.pullback_ofArrows_of_iso`. Next, translate sheafness on both sides into bijectivity of the corresponding `Arrows.toCompatible` maps. The compatible-family subtypes for `g` and for `g ≫ inv f` are equivalent, because the compatibility conditions differ only by composing with the isomorphism `f` and cancelling it. Also, restriction along the isomorphism on sections is bijective via `P.mapIso`. After these identifications, both sides reduce to the same bijectivity statement, and the remaining `convert`/`ext` step checks the two maps coincide pointwise.
declarations.divergence: The mathematical strategy is clean, but the Lean proof is fairly encoded: it introduces an explicit equivalence `e` on compatibility subtypes, uses two abstract bijectivity transport lemmas, and finishes with a pointwise comparison. Understanding it requires tracking several transported maps.

declarations.name: isSheafFor_over_map_op_comp_ofArrows_iff
declarations.nl_statement: For a morphism `p : B ⟶ B'`, a presheaf `P` on `Over B'`, and an `ofArrows` presieve in `Over B`, sheafness of the pulled-back presheaf `((Over.map p).op ⋙ P)` on that presieve is equivalent to sheafness of `P` on the image `ofArrows` presieve obtained by applying `Over.map p` to the arrows.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Reduce both sheaf conditions to bijectivity of the respective `Arrows.toCompatible` maps. Then build an explicit equivalence between the two types of compatible families: the underlying family of elements is unchanged, and compatibility for the composed presheaf is equivalent to compatibility after mapping the arrows with `Over.map p`. The forward direction is the subtle part: from an equality of composites in `Over B'`, pull it back to an equality of underlying arrows in `C`, apply the original compatibility statement in a carefully chosen object of `Over B`, and then transport the resulting equality back by applying `P.map` to a canonical morphism `φ`; the inverse direction is simpler and just applies the target compatibility statement to mapped arrows. After introducing this equivalence, bijectivity of the two `toCompatible` maps is literally the same statement, so the proof ends with `rfl`.
declarations.divergence: Substantial. The underlying idea is transport of compatibility across `Over.map`, but the Lean proof contains heavy categorical bookkeeping (`Over.mk`, `Over.homMk`, `Over.w`, `congr_map`, a manually chosen `φ`, and `cat_disch`) that obscures the simple conceptual statement.

declarations.name: isSheafFor_over_map_op_comp_iff
declarations.nl_statement: Given `p : B ⟶ B'`, a presheaf `P` on `Over B'`, a sieve `R` on `X : Over B`, and an isomorphism `e : (Over.map p).obj X ≅ X'`, sheafness of `((Over.map p).op ⋙ P)` for `R` is equivalent to sheafness of `P` for the pullback along `e.inv` of the functor-pushforward sieve of `R`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Present `R` as an `ofArrows` sieve using `exists_eq_ofArrows`. Then rewrite the target statement step by step: replace both sieves by generated `ofArrows` presentations, use `isSheafFor_pullback_iff` to remove the pullback along the isomorphism `e`, and use `isSheafFor_over_map_op_comp_ofArrows_iff` to move from the composed presheaf on `Over B` to the image arrows in `Over B'`. After these rewrites, the desired equivalence is reduced to an equality of sieves. The final `convert Iff.rfl` asks for this equality, proved by extensionality with two inclusions: one direction unpacks an arrow in the pullback of the functor-pushforward sieve and composes the witnesses to show it lies in the sieve generated by the mapped arrows; the other direction is immediate from the definition of functor pushforward using the basic generator `Sieve.ofArrows_mk`.
declarations.divergence: Moderate. The overall reduction strategy is natural, but the Lean proof compresses several conceptual rewrites into one `rw` chain and the concluding sieve comparison involves nontrivial unpacking of nested existential witnesses.

pr_summary: Refactors ordinal normal-function API toward the general `Order.IsNormal`, replacing older `Ordinal.IsNormal` names/usages with generalized ones and adding deprecated compatibility aliases/wrappers.

declarations.name: Order.IsNormal.monotone
declarations.nl_statement: A normal function between linear orders is monotone.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof is immediate: a normal function is strictly monotone by definition, and every strictly monotone function is monotone.
declarations.divergence: No divergence; it is a one-line projection from `strictMono` followed by the standard coercion to monotonicity.

declarations.name: Ordinal.isFundamentalSequence_of_isNormal
declarations.nl_statement: If `f` is a normal ordinal function and `g` is a fundamental sequence for a successor-limit ordinal `a`, then composing `g` with `f` gives a fundamental sequence for `f a` of the same length.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof packages the three components of a fundamental sequence. Strict monotonicity of the new sequence follows directly from `hf.strictMono` applied to the strict monotonicity of `g`. For cofinality, it chooses an `lsub` presentation of `f a`, rewrites via `hg.cof_eq`, and proves that a certain `lsub` of lower approximants equals `a`; the forward direction uses that each coordinate of the presentation lies below `f a`, hence below some `f b` with `b < a` by rewriting through `IsNormal.blsub_eq` and `lt_blsub_iff`, while the reverse direction shows any `b < a` lies below that `lsub` by extracting a relevant coordinate from strict monotonicity and bounding a `sInf`. Finally, it identifies the `blsub` of the composed sequence with the image of the original `blsub` using `blsub_comp`, then rewrites with `hg.2.2` and `IsNormal.blsub_eq hf ha`.
declarations.divergence: The overall strategy matches the mathematics—normal functions preserve cofinal fundamental sequences—but the Lean proof is fairly indirect, routed through `exists_lsub_cof`, `lsub`, `sInf`, and `blsub` rewrites rather than a transparent high-level argument.

declarations.name: Ordinal.cof_eq_of_isNormal
declarations.nl_statement: A normal function preserves cofinality at successor-limit ordinals: if `a` is successor-limit, then `cof (f a) = cof a`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Pick an arbitrary fundamental sequence for `a`, map it through `f` using `isFundamentalSequence_of_isNormal`, and then compare the cofinalities via the `cof_eq` field of that new fundamental sequence; injectivity of `ord` turns that ordinal equality into cardinal equality.
declarations.divergence: Very direct reduction to the previous theorem; the only indirection is the standard `ord_injective` wrapper.

declarations.name: Ordinal.cof_le_of_isNormal
declarations.nl_statement: For any normal ordinal function `f` and ordinal `a`, the cofinality of `a` is at most the cofinality of `f a`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof splits `a` into the three standard ordinal cases: `0`, successor, or successor-limit. At `0`, the claim is trivial after rewriting `cof_zero`. At successors, both cofinalities simplify to nonzero/one statements, and strict monotonicity gives `0 < f (succ b)`, enough to show the target cardinal is nonzero. At successor-limits, it rewrites using `cof_eq_of_isNormal hf ha`, making the inequality tautological.
declarations.divergence: Close to the natural case split proof; the successor case is a little encoded through cardinal lemmas about nonzeroness.

declarations.name: Ordinal.IsNormal
declarations.nl_statement: Defines the deprecated ordinal-specific notion of a normal function as an alias for the generalized `Order.IsNormal`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is just a definitional wrapper: `Ordinal.IsNormal f` is defined to mean `Order.IsNormal f`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence; it is purely a compatibility alias.

declarations.name: Ordinal.IsNormal.le_set
declarations.nl_statement: Suppose `b` is the least upper bound of a nonempty set `p` of ordinals, expressed by the hypothesis `b ≤ o ↔ ∀ a ∈ p, a ≤ o`. Then for a normal function `f`, `f b ≤ o` iff every `f a` with `a ∈ p` is at most `o`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof first turns the characterization `H₂` into an `IsLUB p b`, then applies `H.map_isLUB` to obtain that `f b` is the least upper bound of `f '' p`. From there, the forward direction says that any point of the image lies below its least upper bound and hence below `o`; the backward direction says that if all image points are at most `o`, then `o` is an upper bound of `f '' p`, so the least upper bound property implies `f b ≤ o`. The final step is a `simpa` rewriting upper-bound membership.
declarations.divergence: More direct than the old recursive proof: it now mirrors the conceptual argument via preservation of least upper bounds almost exactly.

declarations.name: Ordinal.IsNormal.le_set'
declarations.nl_statement: A variant of `IsNormal.le_set` for a set `p : Set α` mapped into ordinals by `g`: if `b` is characterized as the least upper bound of the values `g a` for `a ∈ p`, then `f b ≤ o` iff all `f (g a)` are at most `o`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is reduced by `simpa` to `IsNormal.le_set` applied to the image set `g '' p`, using nonemptiness of the image and the supplied least-upper-bound characterization.
declarations.divergence: Essentially no divergence: it is a straightforward image-set reformulation.

declarations.name: Ordinal.iSup_pow_natCast
declarations.nl_statement: For any positive ordinal `o`, the supremum of the natural powers `o^n` is `o^ω`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof rewrites natural powers as ordinal exponentials `o ^ (n : Ordinal)`. It then splits into the cases `1 < o` and `o = 1`. In the genuinely normal case `1 < o`, it invokes the general theorem `apply_omega0_of_isNormal` for the normal function `a ↦ o^a`. In the remaining case `o = 1`, it proves both inequalities directly by simplifying every term to `1` and observing that `1` appears in the supremum.
declarations.divergence: Follows the standard mathematical proof closely, with only a routine preliminary case split to handle the degenerate base `1`.

declarations.name: Ordinal.apply_omega0_of_isNormal
declarations.nl_statement: For a normal ordinal function `f`, the supremum of the values `f n` over natural numbers is `f ω`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite `ω` as the supremum of the natural ordinals via `iSup_natCast`, then apply normality's `map_iSup` theorem to move `f` across that supremum. The boundedness side condition is discharged by `bddAbove_of_small _`.
declarations.divergence: Very direct; the only non-obvious ingredient is the explicit boundedness argument required by the generalized `map_iSup` API.

declarations.name: Ordinal.iSup_add_natCast
declarations.nl_statement: For any ordinal `o`, the supremum of `o + n` over natural numbers is `o + ω`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is an immediate application of `apply_omega0_of_isNormal` to the normal function `a ↦ o + a`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence beyond naming the appropriate normal function.

declarations.name: Ordinal.iSup_mul_natCast
declarations.nl_statement: For any ordinal `o`, the supremum of `o * n` over natural numbers is `o * ω`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof splits on whether `o = 0`. If `o = 0`, both sides are shown to be zero by simplification and `iSup_eq_zero_iff`. If `o > 0`, it applies `apply_omega0_of_isNormal` to the normal function `a ↦ o * a`, whose normality requires positivity of `o`.
declarations.divergence: A standard degenerate/nondegenerate split, then a direct application of the normal-function theorem.

declarations.name: Ordinal.apply_lt_nfp
declarations.nl_statement: For a normal function `f`, an ordinal lies below the next fixed point `nfp f a` after applying `f` iff it already lay below that fixed point: `f b < nfp f a ↔ b < nfp f a`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof unfolds the single-function fixed-point construction `nfp` into the one-index family version `nfpFamily`, applies the previously proved family theorem `apply_lt_nfpFamily_iff` for the unit-indexed family, and then simplifies the resulting `∀ _ : Unit` quantifier to the original statement.
declarations.divergence: Very direct transport along the definition of `nfp`; the only abstraction is the reuse of the family theorem.

declarations.name: Ordinal.nfp_le_apply
declarations.nl_statement: For a normal function `f`, `nfp f a ≤ f b` iff `nfp f a ≤ b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is obtained formally from `apply_lt_nfp` by converting an equivalence of strict inequalities into one of non-strict inequalities using the linear-order lemma `le_iff_le_iff_lt_iff_lt`.
declarations.divergence: Conceptually straightforward, though the order-theoretic transport lemma hides the elementary duality between `<` and `≤`.

declarations.name: Ordinal.nfp_fp
declarations.nl_statement: Every `nfp f a` is a fixed point of a normal function `f`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is exactly the unit-index specialization of the previously established family fixed-point theorem `nfpFamily_fp`.
declarations.divergence: No meaningful divergence; it is a direct specialization.

declarations.name: Ordinal.apply_le_nfp
declarations.nl_statement: For a normal function `f`, `f b ≤ nfp f a` iff `b ≤ nfp f a`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: For the forward direction, use the general fact `b ≤ f b` coming from strict monotonicity, then compose with the assumed inequality. For the reverse direction, monotonicity of `f` sends `b ≤ nfp f a` to `f b ≤ f (nfp f a)`, and `nfp_fp` rewrites the right-hand side to `nfp f a`.
declarations.divergence: Very close to the textbook argument; the proof is a compact encoding of the two obvious implications.

declarations.name: Ordinal.deriv_fp
declarations.nl_statement: Every value of the derivative `deriv f` of a normal function is a fixed point of `f`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is the specialization of the corresponding family theorem `derivFamily_fp` to the unit-index family containing only `f`.
declarations.divergence: No divergence; it is just specialization.

declarations.name: Ordinal.le_iff_deriv
declarations.nl_statement: For a normal function `f`, the inequality `f a ≤ a` holds exactly when `a` lies in the range of the derivative `deriv f`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unfold `deriv` to `derivFamily` for the unit family, rewrite using the family theorem `le_iff_derivFamily`, and then simplify the resulting statement about all indices of `Unit` to the desired one-function version.
declarations.divergence: Direct reduction to the family theorem; only minor bureaucracy from the unit index remains.

declarations.name: Ordinal.mem_range_deriv
declarations.nl_statement: An ordinal is in the range of `deriv f` exactly when it is a fixed point of the normal function `f`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Membership in the range of `deriv f` is rewritten as `∃ o, deriv f o = a`, then `le_iff_deriv H` converts that existential into the inequality `f a ≤ a`. Finally, since normal functions satisfy `a ≤ f a`, the inequality is equivalent to equality via `H.strictMono.le_apply.ge_iff_eq'`.
declarations.divergence: Very clean: it transparently factors the statement into the range characterization from `le_iff_deriv` plus the standard `a ≤ f a` fact.

declarations.name: Ordinal.isNormal_veblenWith_zero
declarations.nl_statement: If `f` is normal and `f 0 > 0`, then the function sending `o` to `veblenWith f o 0` is itself normal.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: To prove normality, the proof uses `isNormal_iff`: strict monotonicity is already available as `veblenWith_zero_strictMono`. To show this value is below an arbitrary upper bound `a`, it applies `nfpFamily_le`, so it suffices to bound every finite iterate encoded by a list of prior stages. A list induction constructs some index `b < o` such that the fold of the list is bounded by `veblenWith f b 0`; the empty list uses `0 < o`, while the cons step combines the inductive bound with monotonicity in the right argument, monotonicity in the left index, and the key identity `veblenWith f (succ (max _ _)) (veblenWith f b 0) = veblenWith f b 0`, justified by `veblenWith_veblenWith_of_lt hf`. declarations.divergence: The proof follows the intended combinatorial idea—every finite composition of earlier stages is eventually dominated by a single earlier stage—but the Lean realization is somewhat intricate, using list folds, `nfpFamily_le`, and several monotonicity rewrites before the final Veblen absorption identity appears.

pr_summary: This PR removes the TODO by defining the canonical ring isomorphism between Witt vectors modulo the ideal generated by `p` and the base perfect characteristic-`p` ring, using the constant-coefficient map and Teichmüller lifts.

declarations.name: quotientPEquiv
declarations.nl_statement: For a perfect ring `k` of characteristic `p`, the quotient ring `𝕎 k / (p)` is canonically isomorphic to `k`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof identifies the ideal `(p)` with the kernel of the ring homomorphism `constantCoeff : 𝕎 k →+* k`. After rewriting the quotient by `(p)` as the quotient by `ker constantCoeff`, the result follows from the standard `quotientKerEquivOfSurjective`. Surjectivity is witnessed explicitly: for any `r : k`, the Teichmüller Witt vector `teichmuller p r` maps to `r` under `constantCoeff`, proved by `simp`.
declarations.divergence: Very low. The Lean proof is essentially the textbook argument: compute the kernel, invoke the quotient-by-kernel equivalence, and give Teichmüller lifts for surjectivity. The only Lean-specific compression is the `ext; simp [...]` step packaging the kernel computation.

declarations.name: sum_inner
declarations.nl_statement: The inner product is additive in its left argument: `⟪∑ i ∈ s, f i, x⟫ = ∑ i ∈ s, ⟪f i, x⟫`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Fix `x`. The theorem regards `v ↦ ⟪v, x⟫` as a linear map, namely `LinearMap.flip (innerₛₗ 𝕜) x`, and then applies the generic lemma `map_sum` for linear maps. The only subtlety is that because `innerₛₗ` is bundled as linear in the right variable and semilinear in the left, one must flip it to obtain the map linear in the summation variable.
declarations.divergence: Low. The proof is the standard 'a linear map preserves finite sums' argument, though the need to use `LinearMap.flip` reflects the implementation choice for argument order.

declarations.name: inner_sum

declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Fix `x`. Then `w ↦ ⟪x, w⟫` is exactly the linear map `innerₛₗ 𝕜 x`. Applying the standard lemma `map_sum` to this linear map yields the desired identity.
declarations.divergence: Very low. This is a direct application of linearity in the right argument via the bundled map.
