pr_summary: This PR develops the notion of a base of indecomposable positive roots relative to an ordered functional, proves closure and pairwise-separation properties for that base, and uses positive forms to show such roots are linearly independent in crystallographic root systems.

declarations.name: invMonoidHom_comp_invMonoidHom
declarations.nl_statement: For a commutative group, composing the inversion monoid homomorphism with itself is the identity homomorphism.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof extensionality-reduces to elements and then simplifies: applying inversion twice gives back the original element.
declarations.divergence: None; the Lean proof is exactly the obvious argument.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.subset
declarations.nl_statement: Any index that is indecomposable with respect to a set `s` must itself lie in `s`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is immediate from the definition, since membership in `s` is the first conjunct in `IsMulIndecomposable`. The Lean proof is a one-line `aesop`.
declarations.divergence: No mathematical divergence, just automation instead of projecting the first conjunct manually.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.baseOf
declarations.nl_statement: Given a monoid-valued family `v` and an ordered monoid morphism `f`, `baseOf v f` is the set of indices whose values are indecomposable among those indices satisfying `1 < f (v i)`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is a definition: the base is defined to be `IsMulIndecomposable v {i | 1 < f (v i)}`.
declarations.divergence: None; purely definitional.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.baseOf_subset_one_lt
declarations.nl_statement: Every element of `baseOf v f` lies in the positive half-space `{i | 1 < f (v i)}`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is an immediate application of `IsMulIndecomposable.subset` to the defining set of `baseOf`.
declarations.divergence: None.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.image_baseOf_inv_comp_eq
declarations.nl_statement: If the indexing involution corresponds to inversion in the target group, then the image under `v` of the base defined using `invMonoidHom.comp f` is exactly the image under `invMonoidHom ∘ v` of the base defined using `f`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof first establishes one inclusion: an element `v i` coming from the base for `inv ∘ f` is rewritten as `(v (i⁻¹))⁻¹`, and one checks that `i⁻¹` lies in the base for `f`. The key step is to turn a decomposition of `v i⁻¹` into a decomposition of `v i` by inverting the equality and using the compatibility hypothesis `v i⁻¹ = (v i)⁻¹`; indecomposability of `i` then yields triviality of one factor. For the reverse inclusion, the proof applies the first inclusion again after composing with inversion once more, and uses the new lemma that inversion composed with itself is the identity to convert back to equality of images.
declarations.divergence: Mathematically standard, but the Lean proof spends real effort on set-image manipulations and on deriving the reverse inclusion by functorially reapplying the forward implication under inversion.

declarations.name: Submonoid.closure_image_isMulIndecomposable_baseOf
declarations.nl_statement: For a finite family in a monoid, the submonoid generated by all elements in the half-space `1 < f (v i)` is already generated by the indecomposable ones among them.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: One inclusion is immediate because the base is a subset of the half-space. For the converse, fix a positive element `v i` and assume it is not in the closure generated by indecomposables. Consider the set `s` of positive elements outside that closure; by finiteness choose one with minimal `f`-value. Since `i` is not indecomposable, it factors as `v j * v k` with both `j,k` still positive. Ordered cancellation gives `f (v j) < f (v i)` and `f (v k) < f (v i)`, so by minimality both `v j` and `v k` lie in the closure. Their product is then in the closure, contradiction.
declarations.divergence: Very close to the usual minimal-counterexample proof; the only Lean-specific compression is the use of `grind`/automation to extract the nontrivial factorization from failure of indecomposability.

declarations.name: Subgroup.closure_image_isMulIndecomposable_baseOf
declarations.nl_statement: For a finite inversion-stable family in a commutative group, if no `f (v i)` equals `1`, then the subgroup generated by the indecomposable positive part `baseOf v f` already contains the whole image of `v`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof splits all indices into those with `f (v i) > 1` and those with `f (v i) < 1`. The positive half is handled by the previous submonoid-closure lemma. For the negative half, define `f' = inv ∘ f`; then `f (v i) < 1` is equivalent to `1 < f' (v i)`. Using the lemma identifying the base for `f'` with the inverse image of the base for `f`, the closure of the negative half becomes the inverse of the closure generated by the positive base, hence is also contained in the subgroup closure.
declarations.divergence: The mathematical idea is direct, but the Lean proof has noticeable bookkeeping with `image_union`, subgroup/submonoid closure coercions, and rewriting via inversion images.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.pairwise_div_notMem_range
declarations.nl_statement: Suppose every element of a set `s` is indecomposable relative to `t`, and every index is in `t` or its involutive inverse is. Then for distinct `i,j ∈ s`, the quotient `v i / v j` is not in the range of `v`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Assume `v i / v j = v k`. If `k ∈ t`, then `v i = v k * v j`, giving a nontrivial decomposition of `v i`; since `v j ≠ 1`, this contradicts indecomposability of `i`. If instead `k⁻¹ ∈ t`, then rearranging gives `v j = v k⁻¹ * v i`, contradicting indecomposability of `j`.
declarations.divergence: The proof mirrors the case split in the math, but the Lean script packages the contradiction through negating the definition of indecomposable and uses `simp` heavily to normalize the quotient identities.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.pairwise_div_notMem_range'
declarations.nl_statement: If `s` consists of elements indecomposable among the positive half-space `{i | 1 < f (v i)}`, and no `f (v i)` is `1`, then distinct elements of `s` have quotient outside the range of `v`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This specializes the previous lemma. First deduce `v i ≠ 1` from `f (v i) ≠ 1`; next show that for every index `i`, either `i` is positive or `i⁻¹` is positive, since `f (v i)` cannot equal `1`. Then apply `pairwise_div_notMem_range`.
declarations.divergence: Essentially a clean wrapper lemma; only small Lean-specific work is needed to derive the side conditions.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.pairwise_baseOf_div_notMem
declarations.nl_statement: Distinct elements of `baseOf v f` have quotient outside the range of `v`, provided inversion on indices matches inversion on values and no `f (v i)` equals `1`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is the previous lemma applied to `s = baseOf v f` with the identity subset proof.
declarations.divergence: None beyond straightforward specialization.

declarations.name: IsMulIndecomposable.mem_or_inv_mem_closure_baseOf
declarations.nl_statement: For every index `i`, either `v i` or its inverse lies in the submonoid closure generated by the base `baseOf v f`, assuming finiteness and that no `f (v i)` equals `1`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite the closure of the base image as the closure of the whole range using the subgroup-closure theorem. Then split on whether `f (v i)` is greater than or less than `1`. In the first case `v i` itself is in the generating positive image; in the second, `v i⁻¹` is positive and hence lies in the closure.
declarations.divergence: The proof follows the intended dichotomy closely, though it relies on a somewhat non-obvious rewrite through the earlier closure equality.

declarations.name: RootPairing.baseOf_pairwise_pairing_le_zero
declarations.nl_statement: In a crystallographic root pairing, two distinct roots in the base defined by a functional `f` have integer pairing at most zero.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: For distinct base elements `i,j`, the earlier additive indecomposability result says that `P.root i - P.root j` is not a root. Contrapositively, if the pairing `⟪i,j⟫` were positive, a standard root-system lemma would imply that `root i - root j` is a root. Hence the pairing cannot be positive, i.e. it is `≤ 0`.
declarations.divergence: Very direct; Lean expresses it as a `contrapose!` against the root-subtraction lemma.

declarations.name: RootPairing.linearIndepOn_root_baseOf'
declarations.nl_statement: Under an ordered coefficient ring `S` valued in the root pairing, the roots in `baseOf P.root f` are linearly independent over `S`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Restrict to the `S`-span `M₀` of the roots and regard each base root as a vector `v i : M₀`. To prove linear independence in `M`, it suffices to prove `v` is independent in `M₀`. Compose the functional `f` with the subtype to get a strictly positive functional `f'` on these vectors. Choose the positive root form `B`; by the previous lemma together with the comparison lemma between positivity of `B.posForm` and positivity of the pairing, distinct base roots have pairwise nonpositive inner products for `B`. Then invoke the general bilinear-form criterion `linearIndependent_of_pairwise_le_zero` for vectors with positive `f'`-values and pairwise nonpositive angles.
declarations.divergence: Conceptually faithful to the standard argument, but the Lean proof includes structural setup in the root span, transport across subtype maps, and an existence unpacking of the positive form before the final criterion can be applied.

declarations.name: RootPairing.linearIndepOn_root_baseOf
declarations.nl_statement: For a crystallographic root system over a field `R`, the roots in `baseOf P.root f` are linearly independent over `R` when `f` is a nonvanishing `ℚ`-valued functional.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Embed the base roots into the rational root span `P.rootSpan ℚ`. First show these vectors span that space over `ℚ`: every root lies in the additive subgroup closure generated by the base, by the additive closure theorem, hence in the `ℚ`-span of the base roots. Next use `linearIndepOn_root_baseOf'` to obtain `ℚ`-linear independence, producing a basis of `P.rootSpan ℚ`; its cardinality equals `finrank R M` via the existing finrank formula for the root span. Finally show the same family spans all of `M` over `R`, and conclude linear independence over `R` from the cardinality-equals-finrank criterion.
declarations.divergence: The underlying mathematics is standard but the Lean proof is fairly indirect: it routes through the rational root span, additive subgroup closure, basis construction, finrank/cardinality comparisons, and a final `linearIndependent_iff_card_eq_finrank_span` argument rather than a more immediate conceptual proof.

declarations.name: algebraMap_pairingIn'
declarations.nl_statement: If the root pairing is valued in both `T` and `S`, then the value in `S` is the image under `algebraMap T S` of the value in `T`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Apply injectivity of `algebraMap S R` (via `FaithfulSMul`) and compare both sides after mapping to `R`. There they agree by the defining property of `pairingIn` and scalar-tower compatibility.
declarations.divergence: Very direct; the only infrastructure is the standard faithful-scalar-action trick to prove equality before mapping into `R`.

declarations.name: pairingIn_rat
declarations.nl_statement: For a crystallographic root pairing, the rational-valued pairing equals the integer-valued pairing.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is now an immediate specialization of `algebraMap_pairingIn'` from `ℤ` to `ℚ`, after simplifying the algebra maps.
declarations.divergence: None; the refactor makes the proof shorter and more transparent than before.

declarations.name: RootPositiveForm.posForm_apply_root_root_le_zero_iff
declarations.nl_statement: For a positive root form, the inner product of two roots is `≤ 0` if and only if the corresponding pairing value is `≤ 0`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Negate both inequalities and use the already-proved characterization `0 < B.posForm(root i, root j) ↔ 0 < pairingIn i j`. So nonpositivity on one side is equivalent to nonpositivity on the other.
declarations.divergence: None; the Lean proof is the textbook order-theoretic reformulation by `not_le`.

pr_summary: This PR replaces several hand-written proofs with `grind`-based proofs and adds `grind` annotations to supporting simplification lemmas so automation can recover the same case analyses automatically.

declarations.name: SimpleGraph.adj_of_mem_walk_support
declarations.nl_statement: For a nonempty walk `p : G.Walk u v`, every vertex `x` appearing in the support of `p` is adjacent to some vertex `y` that also appears in the support of `p`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof is by induction on the walk. The nil case is impossible because the walk is assumed nonempty. In the cons case, one splits according to whether `x` is the initial vertex of the walk or lies in the tail support. If `x` is the initial vertex, take its immediate neighbor along the first edge. If `x` lies in the tail, then either the tail is nil, in which case `x` is the second vertex and is adjacent back to the start by symmetry, or the tail is nonempty and the induction hypothesis gives a support-vertex adjacent to `x`; this vertex is still in the whole support. The new proof delegates these cases to `grind`, using the characterizations of nil/support and adjacency symmetry.
declarations.divergence: The mathematical structure is still the same induction-and-cases argument, but the explicit witness construction and support manipulations are hidden inside automation, so the Lean script is less transparent than the previous manual proof.

declarations.name: SimpleGraph.Walk.support_cons
declarations.nl_statement: The support of a cons walk is the starting vertex prepended to the support of the tail walk.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is definitionally true: `support` on `cons h p` reduces to `u :: p.support`, so the proof is just `rfl`. The change only adds a `grind` annotation so automation may use the lemma.
declarations.divergence: There is essentially no divergence: the proof is the definitional computation itself.

declarations.name: Finset.max_insert
declarations.nl_statement: The maximum of `insert a s` is `max a s.max` (viewing `a` in `WithBot α`).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: This is an instance of the generic fold theorem for idempotent operations: `Finset.max` is defined as a fold, and inserting one element updates the result by taking the max with that element. The proof is exactly `fold_insert_idem`. The change only marks the lemma for `grind`.
declarations.divergence: Very little divergence: the code directly invokes the underlying fold lemma implementing the definition.

declarations.name: Finset.mem_of_max
declarations.nl_statement: If `s.max = a` for a finset `s`, then `a` is an element of `s`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Proceed by induction on the finset. The empty case is impossible since the max of the empty finset is `⊥`, not a coerced element. For an inserted element `insert b s`, compare the new maximum with `b` and with `s.max`. If the maximum is `b`, then `a = b` and membership is immediate. Otherwise the maximum comes from `s`, and the induction hypothesis shows `a ∈ s`, hence `a ∈ insert b s`. The `grind` proof reconstructs this analysis using `max_insert` and injectivity of coercions (`WithBot.coe_eq_coe`).
declarations.divergence: The underlying argument is a standard induction on insert, but the crucial branch analysis on `max` is compressed into automation; one can infer the idea, though not as directly as in the former explicit proof.

declarations.name: Set.uIoc_of_le
declarations.nl_statement: If `a ≤ b`, then the unordered open-closed interval `Ι a b` is just the ordinary interval `Ioc a b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unfold `uIoc` as `Ioc (min a b) (max a b)` and simplify `min` and `max` using the assumption `a ≤ b`. The proof is `simp [uIoc, h]`. The change only adds a `grind` annotation.
declarations.divergence: No real divergence: the Lean proof is exactly the obvious simplification.

declarations.name: Set.uIoc_of_ge
declarations.nl_statement: If `b ≤ a`, then the unordered open-closed interval `Ι a b` is `Ioc b a`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again unfold `uIoc` and simplify `min` and `max` under the assumption `b ≤ a`, yielding `Ioc b a`. The proof is `simp [uIoc, h]`. The change only adds a `grind` annotation.
declarations.divergence: No real divergence: the Lean proof is the direct simplification of the definition.

declarations.name: Set.eq_of_notMem_uIoc_of_notMem_uIoc
declarations.nl_statement: Assume `a ≤ c` and `b ≤ c`. If `a` is not in `Ι b c` and `b` is not in `Ι a c`, then `a = b`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Expand the two nonmembership assumptions using the characterization of `notMem_uIoc`. Each assumption says either the point lies at or below both endpoints, or it lies strictly above both endpoints. Under the extra bounds `a ≤ c` and `b ≤ c`, the ‘strictly above `c`’ alternatives are impossible, so one obtains both `a ≤ b` and `b ≤ a`, hence equality by antisymmetry. The old proof performed the four-case analysis explicitly and discharged impossible branches via contradictions with `ha` or `hb`; `grind` now does this reasoning automatically.
declarations.divergence: The proof idea is simple and well matched to automation here; the only loss is that the contradiction/antisymmetry steps are implicit rather than written out.

pr_summary: Adds three basic integer-value facts about π in `Real.Pi.Bounds`: its floor is 3, its ceiling is 4, and its nearest integer (via `round`) is 3.

declarations.name: Real.floor_pi_eq_three
declarations.nl_statement: The floor of π is 3.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof applies `Int.floor_eq_iff`, reducing the claim to showing `3 ≤ π` and `π < 4`. The lower bound is obtained directly from the existing theorem `pi_gt_three` by taking `le`, and the upper bound is discharged by `pi_lt_four` after `norm_num` simplifies the arithmetic side condition `π < 3 + 1`.
declarations.divergence: Very direct: the Lean proof exactly follows the textbook characterization of the floor and plugs in the standard bounds `3 < π < 4` with only minor normalization.

declarations.name: Real.ceil_pi_eq_four
declarations.nl_statement: The ceiling of π is 4.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof uses `Int.ceil_eq_iff`, so it is enough to prove `4 - 1 < π` and `π ≤ 4`. After `norm_num` turns the first inequality into `3 < π`, the theorem `pi_gt_three` finishes it; the second is `pi_lt_four.le`.
declarations.divergence: Again essentially identical to the mathematical argument from `3 < π < 4`; the only Lean-specific ingredient is invoking the library iff for ceilings and normalizing `4 - 1`.

declarations.name: Real.round_pi_eq_three
declarations.nl_statement: Rounding π to the nearest integer gives 3.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: The proof rewrites `round π` as `⌊π + 1/2⌋` via `round_eq`, and then proves that this floor is 3 using `Int.floor_eq_iff`. For the lower bound, `grw [← pi_gt_three]` changes the goal to the existing fact `3 < π`, after which `norm_num` handles the arithmetic around `π + 1/2`. For the upper bound, `grw [pi_lt_d2]` replaces `π` by the sharper estimate `π < 3.15`; `norm_num` then checks that `3.15 + 1/2 < 4`, i.e. `π + 1/2 < 3 + 1`.
declarations.divergence: The core idea is natural—show `π` is closer to 3 than to 4 by proving `3 ≤ π + 1/2 < 4`—but the Lean proof is a bit less transparent than the previous two because it routes through `round_eq`, uses `grw` rewrites in inequalities, and relies on the auxiliary decimal bound `pi_lt_d2` rather than stating the final arithmetic comparison explicitly.

pr_summary: This PR is a pure rename cleanup for orthogonal/star projection lemmas, updating downstream uses and adding deprecated aliases for the old names.

declarations.name: Submodule.orthogonalProjection_apply_eq_linearProjOfIsCompl
declarations.nl_statement: If a submodule `K` has an orthogonal projection, then for every vector `x`, the value of `K.orthogonalProjection x` is exactly the value of the linear projection obtained from the complementary decomposition `K ⊕ Kᗮ`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Fix the complement witness `IsCompl K Kᗮ`. Rewrite `x` as the sum of the two complementary projections using `projection_add_projection_eq_self`. After expanding `IsCompl.projection_apply`, the term coming from the `K`-projection is unchanged because `orthogonalProjection x` lies in `K`, while the term coming from the orthogonal complement vanishes because `orthogonalProjection x` is orthogonal to `Kᗮ`. What remains is exactly the desired equality.
declarations.divergence: Very direct: the proof follows the standard decomposition `x = proj_K x + proj_{Kᗮ} x` and checks the two pieces by the defining properties of orthogonal projection. The only Lean-specific wrinkle is the initial `conv_lhs` rewrite and the use of simp lemmas to discharge membership/orthogonality facts.

declarations.name: Submodule.coe_orthogonalProjection_eq_linearProjOfIsCompl
declarations.nl_statement: If `K` has an orthogonal projection, then the linear map underlying `K.orthogonalProjection : E →ₗ[𝕜] K` is equal to the linear projection associated to the complementary pair `K` and `Kᗮ`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use extensionality of linear maps. For each `x`, reduce to the previous pointwise theorem `orthogonalProjection_apply_eq_linearProjOfIsCompl`.
declarations.divergence: Essentially none: this is the textbook promotion from pointwise equality to equality of linear maps via `LinearMap.ext`.

declarations.name: Submodule.coe_starProjection_eq_isComplProjection
declarations.nl_statement: If `K` has an orthogonal projection, then the linear map underlying the star projection onto `K` coincides with the `IsCompl.projection` coming from the decomposition by `K` and `Kᗮ`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Unfold `starProjection`, rewrite the orthogonal projection part using `coe_orthogonalProjection_eq_linearProjOfIsCompl`, and simplify the definition of `IsCompl.projection`. The equality is then by reflexive simplification.
declarations.divergence: Very small: the proof is just definitional unfolding plus one previously established equality. It mirrors the intended identification almost perfectly.

declarations.name: LinearMap.IsSymmetricProjection.le_iff_range_le_range
declarations.nl_statement: For symmetric projection endomorphisms `p` and `q`, one has `p ≤ q` in the positive-operator order if and only if `range p ≤ range q`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: For the forward direction, start from positivity of `q - p`, so `0 ≤ re ⟪(q-p)a,a⟫` for every `a`. Rewrite the inner products using the fact that a symmetric projection satisfies `re ⟪T a, a⟫ = ‖T a‖^2`, and for `a ∈ range p` replace `p a` by `a` using idempotence. This turns the inequality into `‖a‖ ≤ ‖q a‖`. Next represent `q` as the star projection of some submodule `U`. The norm characterization `U.mem_iff_norm_starProjection` says that equality of `‖q a‖` and `‖a‖` forces `a ∈ U`, and the opposite inequality needed for equality is the standard contraction estimate for star projections. Hence `a ∈ range q`, giving `range p ≤ range q`. For the reverse implication, invoke the earlier result that the difference of symmetric projections is positive when the ranges are nested.
declarations.divergence: The mathematical idea is clean, but the Lean proof is moderately compressed: it packages the key inner-product-to-norm computation in a local helper `hh`, uses a large `simp_rw` to convert positivity into a norm inequality, and then finishes through the submodule/star-projection characterization of `q`. The structure still matches the conceptual argument, but several steps are bundled into automation-heavy rewrites.

declarations.name: Submodule.starProjection_le_starProjection_iff
declarations.nl_statement: For submodules `U` and `V` with orthogonal projections, `U.starProjection ≤ V.starProjection` in the positive-operator order if and only if `U ≤ V`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Translate the operator inequality on star projections to the corresponding inequality on their underlying linear maps. Apply the previous theorem for symmetric projections to replace operator order by inclusion of ranges. Then identify the range of a star projection with the original submodule via `coe_starProjection_eq_isComplProjection` and `IsCompl.projection_range`. After these identifications, the statement is exactly `U ≤ V`.
declarations.divergence: Direct and conceptually tidy. The Lean proof is a single `simp_rw`, but each rewrite corresponds exactly to the intended chain of equivalences: order on projections, range inclusion, and range of the projection equals the submodule.

pr_summary: This PR adds two sign lemmas for `ArchimedeanClass.stdPart` and makes an internal quotient-order connectivity lemma private again, with a small eta-expansion in the `LinearOrder` instance to use that private proof.

declarations.name: FiniteResidueField.ordConnected_preimage_mk'
declarations.nl_statement: For any residue-class `x` in `FiniteResidueField K`, the set of finite elements whose quotient image is `x` is order-connected: whenever two elements lie in that fiber, every element between them lies in the same fiber.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Fix a class `x`, and unpack `Set.OrdConnected`. A final funext/simpa packages the pointwise derivative identity into equality of functions.

declarations.name: iteratedDeriv_comp_const_sub
declarations.nl_statement: For any n, f, and s, the n-th iterated derivative of z ↦ f (s - z) is t ↦ (-1)^n • iteratedDeriv n f (s - t).

pr_summary: This PR tidies the Rayleigh quotient file by adding additivity of the Rayleigh quotient, simplifying some coercions and scalar expressions, and slightly streamlining a local-extremum-to-eigenvector proof without changing the underlying mathematical arguments.

declarations.name: ContinuousLinearMap.rayleighQuotient_add

declarations.name: IsSelfAdjoint.eq_smul_self_of_isLocalExtrOn_real
declarations.nl_statement: If T is self-adjoint on a real complete inner product space and x₀ is a local extremum of the quadratic form x ↦ ⟪Tx,x⟫ on the sphere of radius ‖x₀‖, then T x₀ is a scalar multiple of x₀, with scalar equal to the Rayleigh quotient of T at x₀.

If x₀ = 0, the conclusion is trivial. If b = 0, then a ≠ 0, so the relation forces x₀ = 0, contradicting the nonzero case; hence b ≠ 0. Solve the linear dependence for T x₀, obtaining T x₀ = (-b⁻¹ a) • x₀ by linear combination. To identify the scalar, apply the inner product with x₀ to both sides and simplify: since the extremum is on the sphere centered at 0, the resulting coefficient is exactly the Rayleigh quotient. Lean now packages the last step as `simpa ... using congr_arg (fun x => ⟪x, x₀⟫) hc`, replacing an older two-step `have` plus `exact`.
declarations.divergence: Low: the proof closely follows the standard Lagrange-multiplier argument and scalar identification; the only mildly nontransparent part is the `linear_combination` step and some simp/field normalization.

declarations.nl_statement: If T is self-adjoint on a complete inner product space over ℝ or ℂ and x₀ is a local extremum of the quadratic form on the sphere of radius ‖x₀‖, then T x₀ equals the Rayleigh quotient at x₀, viewed as a scalar in the base field, times x₀.

declarations.name: LinearMap.IsSymmetric.hasEigenvalue_iSup_of_finiteDimensional
declarations.nl_statement: On a nontrivial finite-dimensional inner product space, a symmetric linear map has an eigenvalue equal to the supremum of its Rayleigh quotient over all nonzero vectors.

declarations.divergence: Very low: a direct finite-dimensional compactness/minimization argument with little Lean overhead.

pr_summary: This PR adds basic compatibility lemmas showing that the intrinsic star on linear maps is given by conjugation with `starLinearEquiv`, and that it commutes with `toSpanSingleton` and `smulRight`.

declarations.nl_statement: For a linear map `f : E →ₗ[R] F`, its intrinsic star equals composition of `f` on the left and right with the star linear equivalence: `star f = starLinearEquiv.toLinearMap ∘ₛₗ f ∘ₛₗ starLinearEquiv.toLinearMap`.

declarations.divergence: No divergence; the Lean proof is literally the definitional equality corresponding to the mathematical statement.

declarations.name: LinearMap.IntrinsicStar.starLinearEquiv_eq
declarations.nl_statement: The `starLinearEquiv` on the linear-map space `E →ₗ[R] F` is exactly the arrow congruence induced by `starLinearEquiv` on source and target.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again the proof is `rfl`: once the star structure on linear maps is unfolded, the resulting linear equivalence is definitionally the same as `arrowCongr (starLinearEquiv R) (starLinearEquiv R)`.

declarations.name: LinearMap.intrinsicStar_toSpanSingleton
declarations.nl_statement: Taking intrinsic star commutes with the linear map `toSpanSingleton`: the star of `toSpanSingleton S E a` is `toSpanSingleton S E (star a)`.

pr_summary: This PR strengthens `Subgroup.closure_pow_le` by removing the unnecessary assumption `n ≠ 0`, and correspondingly simplifies the proof of `Subgroup.closure_pow` to use the stronger lemma directly.

declarations.name: Subgroup.closure_pow_le
declarations.nl_statement: For any natural number `n`, the subgroup closure of the pointwise power set `s ^ n` is contained in the closure of `s`.

Concretely, the Lean proof rewrites `pow_zero`, then proves `x = 1` by transporting the hypothesis through `Subgroup.closure_eq_bot_iff` instantiated with the fact `{1}` has trivial closure. In the inductive step, rewrite `s^(n+1)` as `s^n * s`, apply the previously established `closure_mul_le` to bound the closure by `closure (s^n) ⊔ closure s`, use the induction hypothesis on the first term, and finish with `sup_idem`.
declarations.divergence: The mathematical idea is direct, but the base case is less transparent in Lean than on paper: instead of simply observing that `closure ({1}) = ⊥` and hence every element is `1`, the proof uses `simp only`, a `suffices`, and a somewhat compact `simpa [Subgroup.closure_eq_bot_iff.mpr ?_] using hx` step with an implicit subproof. The successor case is very clean and follows the intended argument almost verbatim.

declarations.nl_statement: If `1 ∈ s` and `n ≠ 0`, then the closure of `s ^ n` equals the closure of `s`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: One inclusion is the strengthened lemma `closure_pow_le`, giving `closure (s^n) ≤ closure s` for all `n`. For the reverse inclusion, because `1 ∈ s` and `n ≠ 0`, every element of `s` lies in `s^n` via `subset_pow hs hn`; monotonicity of closure then gives `closure s ≤ closure (s^n)`. The two inequalities are combined with `antisymm`.
declarations.divergence: This proof is extremely direct. The Lean term `closure_pow_le.antisymm <| by gcongr; exact subset_pow hs hn` is terse, but it mirrors the mathematical two-sided inclusion argument almost perfectly and benefits from the stronger preceding lemma.

declarations.divergence: Low. The calc block follows the standard partition-of-s-into-(s∩t) and (s\t) argument very directly; the only opacity is that each justification is hidden behind grind rather than named lemmas.

declarations.name: le_card_sdiff
declarations.nl_statement: For finsets s and t, the natural-number difference #t - #s is at most #(t \ s).
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: With the new equality available, the result is immediate: #t - #s = #(t \ s) - #(s \ t), and subtracting a natural number can only decrease a quantity, so this is at most #(t \ s). The Lean proof is just by grind, which reconstructs this automatically.
declarations.divergence: Moderate-low. Mathematically the proof is very short and natural, but the Lean term is fully implicit: unlike the previous explicit calc chain, it relies on grind to find and use the new equality plus monotonicity of subtraction.

declarations.name: continuousAt_floor
declarations.nl_statement: If `x` is not an integer (`x ≠ ⌊x⌋`), then `floor` is continuous at `x`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Take the interval `Ico ⌊x⌋ (⌊x⌋+1)` on which `floor` is constant. The hypothesis implies `x` lies strictly above the left endpoint, and `lt_floor_add_one` gives the upper bound, so this interval is a neighborhood of `x`. Restrict the continuous-on result to that neighborhood.
declarations.divergence: Very close to the usual proof. Lean expresses 'is a neighborhood' via `Ico_mem_nhds`, but the structure is exactly the mathematical one.

declarations.name: continuousOn_floor_compl_range
declarations.nl_statement: `floor` is continuous on the complement of the integer range.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: At each point outside `range Int.cast`, show it cannot equal its floor, then apply `continuousAt_floor` and turn pointwise continuity into `ContinuousOn`.
declarations.divergence: Direct pointwise packaging of the previous lemma; only the set-complement bookkeeping is Lean-specific.

declarations.name: continuousAt_ceil
declarations.nl_statement: If `x` is not an integer, then `ceil` is continuous at `x`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use the interval `Ioc (⌈x⌉-1) ⌈x⌉` on which `ceil` is constant. The upper neighborhood condition comes from `le_ceil x`; if equality held there, one would get `x = ⌊x⌋`, contradicting the hypothesis. The lower condition is `ceil_lt_add_one`. Thus this interval is a neighborhood of `x`, and continuity follows from `continuousOn_ceil`.
declarations.divergence: Mathematically standard, but slightly less transparent than the floor case because the proof must convert the hypothesis `x ≠ ⌊x⌋` into the strict inequality `x < ⌈x⌉` by a short contradiction argument.

declarations.name: continuousOn_ceil_compl_range
declarations.nl_statement: `ceil` is continuous on the complement of the integer range.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: For a point outside the integer range, deduce it is not equal to its floor, apply `continuousAt_ceil`, and package the result as continuity on the set.
declarations.divergence: A straightforward corollary of `continuousAt_ceil` with only routine set-membership reasoning.

declarations.name: continuousOn_fract
declarations.nl_statement: On each interval `Ico n (n+1)`, the fractional-part map is continuous.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use `fract x = x - floor x`. The identity is continuous, and `floor` is continuous on the interval as a map into the discrete space `ℤ`, hence also as an `α`-valued locally constant map after composing with the coercion from `ℤ`. Subtract the two continuous-on maps.
declarations.divergence: The mathematics is standard; the Lean proof’s only extra layer is the explicit use of `continuous_of_discreteTopology` to pass from `ℤ`-valued continuity to continuity after coercion.

declarations.name: continuousAt_fract
declarations.nl_statement: If `x` is not an integer, then `fract` is continuous at `x`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Again write `fract = id - floor`; the identity is continuous everywhere, and `floor` is continuous at such `x` by `continuousAt_floor`, after composing with the discrete-topology continuity of the integer inclusion. Then subtract.
declarations.divergence: Direct and conceptually clean; only the discrete-topology coercion is slightly implementation-specific.

declarations.name: tendsto_round_nhdsGE_pure
declarations.nl_statement: Approaching `x` from the right, `round` tends to the constant value `round x`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Rewrite `round` using `round_eq'` as the composition of `y ↦ floor y` at `y = 2x` with the integer map `n ↦ (n+1)/2`. Show that doubling sends the right-neighborhood filter `𝓝[≥] x` into `𝓝[≥] (2x)` using monotonicity of addition, apply the known right-limit of `floor`, then compose with the pure map on integers.
declarations.divergence: The argument is mathematically natural, but the proof is filter-heavy and expressed through composition of `Tendsto` statements. It mirrors the intended one-sided constancy result, though less transparently than an interval-based argument might.

declarations.name: tendsto_round_nhdsLT_pure_half_ceil
declarations.nl_statement: Approaching `x` from the left, `round` tends to the constant value `⌈2x⌉ / 2`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: As above, rewrite `round` by `round_eq'` and observe that doubling carries `𝓝[<] x` to `𝓝[<] (2x)`. Then use the left-limit formula for `floor`, namely that `floor y` tends to `⌈y⌉-1` from the left, and finally simplify `((⌈2x⌉-1)+1)/2` to `⌈2x⌉/2` by arithmetic.
declarations.divergence: Again mathematically reasonable but fairly encoded in filter combinators (`tendsto_pure`, `filter_upwards`) and simplification. The underlying idea is simple; the Lean presentation is moderately indirect.

declarations.name: continuousAt_round
declarations.nl_statement: If `2 * fract x ≠ 1` (so `x` is not a half-integer tie point), then `round` is continuous at `x`.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Use the characterization of continuity at a point by matching left and right one-sided limits. The right limit is `round x` by `tendsto_round_nhdsGE_pure`, while the left limit is `⌈2x⌉/2` by `tendsto_round_nhdsLT_pure_half_ceil`. The hypothesis lets you identify this left-limit value with `round x` via `round_eq_half_ceil_two_mul`, so both sides agree and continuity follows.
declarations.divergence: The conceptual proof is clear and standard: compute left and right limits and compare them. Lean’s execution uses filter order relations and monotonicity lemmas, which adds some boilerplate but does not obscure the main idea too much.

declarations.name: continuousOn_round
declarations.nl_statement: `round` is continuous on the set of points where `2 * fract x ≠ 1`, i.e. away from half-integers.
declarations.nl_proof_sketch: Pointwise apply `continuousAt_round` and reinterpret it as continuity within the subset.
declarations.divergence: None beyond routine packaging of a pointwise continuity statement.
